Republican Senator Discloses Her Husband Committed Suicide

Republican Senator Deb Fischer (R-NE) announced on Friday that her husband, Bruce Fischer, died by suicide. Initially, the family had stated he had "passed away peacefully" on November 22, but further investigation revealed he took his own life. Fischer described Bruce as her "partner in life, my greatest source of strength, and the heart of our family." Bruce Fischer was 76 years old and a lifelong rancher in the Nebraska Sandhills. The couple, married since 1972, had three sons and six grandchildren. The family said they would not provide further details or comment on Bruce’s death.

Bruce Fischer made national headlines in January 2025 for refusing to shake the hand of then-Vice President Kamala Harris during his wife’s swearing-in ceremony. The incident, captured on video, showed Bruce holding a Bible and a cane, and responding only with a "thank you" when Harris extended her hand.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and The Hill both mention Bruce Fischer was 76 years old at the time of his death, while The New York Post and The Daily Caller state he was 75. The Daily Wire and The Hill refer to the initial announcement of his death as occurring on November 22, while The New York Post and The Daily Caller note the initial statement was made on Monday, which is November 22. The Daily Wire and The Hill mention Bruce was a "lifelong rancher" and "conservationist," while The New York Post and The Daily Caller describe him as a "rancher" and "conservationist dedicated to responsible resource stewardship." The Daily Wire and The Hill attribute the handshaking incident to January 2025, while The Daily Caller and The New York Post specify the event occurred in January 2025. The Daily Wire and The Hill mention Bruce and Deb met at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, while The Daily Caller and The New York Post also note this detail. The Daily Wire and The Hill state the family would not provide further details, while The Daily Caller and The New York Post also note this.

Sources The Daily Wire · New York Post · The Daily Caller · The Hill · Washington Examiner · CBS News

No source labeled left covered this story.

NY Senate leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, first woman in the role, dies at 76

New York State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, the first woman to lead the chamber, died Friday, her office confirmed. She was 76. Stewart-Cousins was reelected by her constituents on Nov. 3 and retained as Senate Democratic leader mid-month. Her death was announced by Mike Murphy, a spokesperson for the Senate's Democratic majority, though the cause and location were not disclosed. Stewart-Cousins was a prominent advocate for progressive policies, including legalizing marijuana, strengthening gun control, and advancing voting rights and police accountability measures. She also led efforts to secure voter approval of a state constitutional amendment protecting abortion rights. Her leadership marked a significant shift in New York's political landscape, breaking the so-called "three men in a room" tradition of decision-making.

Stewart-Cousins, a resident of Yonkers, had a long career in public service, including roles as a teacher, sales and marketing professional, and local government official. She was the first African American woman to lead the New York State Senate and the first woman to hold the position. Her leadership was widely praised by political figures across the spectrum, including Governor Kathy Hochul, former Governor Andrew Cuomo, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Tributes highlighted her impact on reproductive rights, education, and civil rights, as well as her role in advancing legislation such as the Eric Garner Anti-Chokehold Act.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that Stewart-Cousins was found dead in her Yonkers home on Friday morning and that her daughter tried to contact her on Thursday night before requesting a welfare check. This detail is not included in ABC News, Newsweek, The Hill, Washington Examiner, or Just The News. Additionally, FOX News states she was first elected to the state senate in 2007, while ABC News and The Hill note she was first elected in 2006. Newsweek and The Hill mention she was the first African American woman to lead the Senate, while FOX News and Washington Examiner refer to her as the first Black woman to hold the role. ABC News and The Hill attribute her role as the first woman and first Black woman to the Senate to her own leadership, while FOX News and Washington Examiner attribute it to her being the first Black woman.

Sources ABC News · Newsweek · The Hill · Washington Examiner · Just The News · FOX News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Biden’s first-week book sales lag behind Obama’s and Clinton’s

Former President Joe Biden’s memoir, *Promise Me, America*, sold approximately 21,000 copies in its first week, according to Circana, as reported by multiple outlets. The book topped the New York Times nonfiction bestseller list. Biden’s limited public appearances to promote the book, due to his Stage 4 prostate cancer diagnosis, were noted by several outlets. The memoir’s sales were compared to those of former presidents Barack Obama and Bill Clinton, with Obama’s *A Promised Land* and Clinton’s *My Life* both surpassing 1 million copies in their first weeks.

The book’s publisher, Little, Brown and Company, expressed pride in its performance on the bestseller list. Some outlets mentioned that Biden’s memoir underperformed compared to other former first ladies’ memoirs, such as Michelle Obama’s *Becoming* and Hillary Clinton’s *What Happened*, which each sold over 1 million copies. The New York Post noted that Biden’s book sold 21,000 copies despite a $10 million advance, and some former aides expressed disappointment with the sales figures.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and Just The News both report that Biden’s memoir sold 21,000 copies in its first week, but only Just The News and the New York Post mention that Obama’s *A Promised Land* sold over 800,000 copies in the first 24 hours. The Guardian and ABC News also note this figure, while FOX News and the New York Post provide the same detail. The New York Post and the Guardian mention that Biden’s book sold 21,000 copies, while the Washington Examiner and Just The News do not specify the time frame for Obama’s sales. The New York Post and the Guardian also note that Jill Biden’s memoir, *View from the East Wing*, sold around 46,000 copies, a detail not included in the Washington Examiner or Just The News accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · Just The News · FOX News · The Guardian · ABC News · New York Post

No source labeled center covered this story.

US military disables commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman for attempting to bypass naval blockade after leaving Iran

The U.S. military disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday, according to U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), for attempting to bypass a naval blockade after departing from an Iranian port. The ship, the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer, left Bandar Abbas, a major port city on Iran's southern coast, before being struck by precision munitions. The strike disabled the ship's propulsion, and the civilian crew was unharmed. CENTCOM released a video showing the projectile hitting the ship's stern and causing an explosion. The incident occurred on November 26, 2026.

President Donald Trump commented on the event during a Thanksgiving Day call with U.S. service members, stating that victory in the Iran conflict would come "whenever I want it." He emphasized the U.S. was giving Iran every chance to make a deal to save lives but expressed doubt about Iran's willingness to comply. Trump also mentioned that the U.S. had launched 150 missiles to intercept threats targeting commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and Just The News both state that the ship attempted to run the U.S. naval blockade after leaving an Iranian port, while FOX News and the New York Post describe the ship as attempting to slip through the naval blockade of all Iranian ports. The Washington Examiner and Just The News mention that the blockade has been in place since mid-July, while FOX News and the New York Post do not specify the start date of the blockade. The New York Post and FOX News include additional details about Trump's Thanksgiving Day remarks and his comments on missile launches and international involvement, which are not present in the Washington Examiner or Just The News accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · FOX News · New York Post · Just The News · CBS News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment

A pregnant inmate, Rebecca Taylor, 26, escaped from custody in New Mexico after taking control of a corrections department vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment. The New Mexico Corrections Department confirmed the escape, stating that Taylor was not restrained due to her pregnancy. She was transported with another inmate, who was also returning from a prenatal appointment. The vehicle was later found in an Albuquerque neighborhood, along with her prison jumpsuit, but Taylor remains at large. The department has initiated a multi-agency search for Taylor, and all prisons in New Mexico were placed on lockdown following the incident.

The escape occurred when the transport team stopped for food in Albuquerque. According to multiple reports, Taylor unbuckled herself and drove away while the driver was outside the vehicle. The other inmate was able to flee the car and was subsequently recaptured. The corrections department noted that the vehicle was located via GPS, but Taylor was not inside when it was found. Authorities have urged the public not to approach Taylor and to report any sightings immediately.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that another inmate was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control, while New York Post and CBS News also mention that the other inmate escaped but was recaptured. FOX News does not specify whether the other inmate was recaptured. New York Post and CBS News mention a Whataburger stop, while BBC refers to a food stop in Albuquerque. CBS News states that Taylor was not restrained due to her pregnancy, a detail also included in BBC and FOX News. New York Post and CBS News provide details about Taylor's criminal history, including theft and burglary charges, while FOX News attributes this information to the New Mexico Corrections Department. BBC mentions that the prison where Taylor was held will remain on "modified movement," while the other accounts do not specify this.

Sources BBC · New York Post · CBS News · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed frustration with the U.S. stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, calling Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" "strange." In an interview with the BBC, Zelensky likened the remark to calling Adolf Hitler a friend during World War II, emphasizing that Putin is an "aggressor and a killer" who cannot be a friend. Zelensky also criticized the U.S. for delays in delivering anti-ballistic missiles, which he said are costing Ukrainian lives. He urged the U.S. to apply more pressure on Russia to end the war, which has lasted nearly five years. Peace talks have stalled, with Zelensky expressing hope for renewed negotiations in December. Meanwhile, Trump has continued to describe his relationship with Putin as positive, claiming he has urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression" and that a peace deal is "a strong possibility."

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports Zelensky called Trump's remark "strange" and compared it to calling Hitler a friend, while ABC News and CBS News include similar comparisons. The Guardian and Newsweek do not mention Zelensky's specific comparison to Hitler. The Guardian focuses on Kushner's interview and his views on Putin, which are not covered in the other accounts. The Hill and Newsweek mention Zelensky's frustration with the U.S. delay in delivering Patriot missiles, while the BBC and CBS News include this detail as well. The Guardian and Newsweek do not mention Zelensky's comments on the U.S. satellite communication issue, which is included in the BBC account. The Guardian and Newsweek also include details about the Libya strike and the return of children from Russia, which are not present in the other accounts.

Sources BBC · ABC News · The Hill · CBS News · The Guardian · Newsweek

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

NYC Mayor Mamdani has 'successful' surgery on torn Achilles tendon

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani underwent a "successful" surgery on Friday for his torn Achilles tendon. The procedure began at 11:33 a.m. and concluded at 12:42 p.m. He was discharged from the hospital and is now resting comfortably at Gracie Mansion. First Deputy Mayor Dean Fuleihan is leading day-to-day operations while Mamdani recovers. The injury occurred during a soccer match against the City Hall press corps last week. Mamdani said he "did not stretch" before taking to the pitch and that he tore the tendon soon after scoring a goal.

Mamdani first appeared injured last week at a morning press conference where he disclosed his injury. He injured his Achilles while playing a soccer game against New York City’s press corps. He said he forgot the stretch before hitting the field, telling reporters, “I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch, and I forgot that I was 35 and soon after I tore my Achilles.” He added that he will be in a boot for six to eight weeks and will play soccer in about nine months. Due to the surgery, he will also not be able to attend the rescheduled Macy’s Thanksgiving parade.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and The Hill both report that the surgery took place on Friday, starting at 11:33 a.m. and ending at 12:42 p.m. The Hill and Washington Examiner state that the procedure took roughly 70 minutes, while ABC News does not specify the duration. The Hill and The New York Post mention that Mamdani will miss the rescheduled Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, while ABC News does not mention the parade at all. The Washington Examiner and The New York Post attribute the statement about the surgery duration to Joe Calvello, while The Hill also attributes the same statement to Calvello. The New York Post includes a quote from Mamdani referencing Jayson Tatum’s injury, which is not mentioned in the other accounts.

Sources ABC News · The Hill · Washington Examiner · New York Post

No source labeled left covered this story.

Zeldin: No airborne lead detected in Iowa a day after Army blast

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reported no airborne lead was detected in the region following the Army’s controlled detonation of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin stated that air monitors recorded zero detect of airborne lead since the detonation. The agency collected over 1,000 samples of air, soil, and water after the blast, with results expected as early as Friday. The operation was conducted to neutralize deteriorating explosives deemed too dangerous to transport. Federal officials declared the detonation a success, lifting a shelter-in-place order and allowing residents to resume normal activities.

The EPA also reported that no increase in lead levels was found in drinking water sources tested after the detonation. The agency emphasized that it is continuing its environmental assessment, comparing samples collected before and after the event. President Trump praised the operation, calling it a success and stating residents were “100% safe.” The Army cited the need to prevent an uncontrolled explosion involving the unstable material, which had been stored for over two decades.

Where the accounts differ

The The Hill and FOX News both report that no airborne lead was detected, but FOX News adds that Zeldin described the results as a “best-case scenario” and that the EPA released its first laboratory results on Friday night. CBS News and the New York Post mention that the EPA collected over 1,600 samples before and after the detonation, while the New York Post also notes that the Army had planned the detonation for November and had communicated with the EPA and local officials. The The Hill and FOX News differ in the number of samples collected, with The Hill stating over 1,000 samples were collected after the detonation, while FOX News mentions over 1,000 samples were collected following the blast and over 1,600 before.

Sources The Hill · FOX News · CBS News · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Holiday scammers target older Americans, often returning to exploit them multiple times, experts warn

Scammers are increasingly targeting older Americans during the holiday season, often returning to exploit the same victims multiple times, according to recent reports. Federal authorities and consumer protection groups warn that the holidays are a particularly lucrative time for fraud, as older adults engage in more online shopping, travel, and charitable giving. A November 2026 AARP survey found that 84% of U.S. adults had encountered a scam or fraud attempt ahead of the holidays, with nearly 39% of those who purchased something through an online advertisement reporting they were scammed. The Federal Trade Commission reported that Americans ages 60 and older lost around $3 billion in fraud losses in 2025, with older victims losing as much as $119.5 billion last year.

Experts note that scammers often return to the same victims, using tactics such as posing as officials promising to recover funds or sharing personal information on the black market. The Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network said that after a successful scam, some fraudsters share victims' personal information, allowing other criminals to target them again with different schemes. AARP's Amy Nofziger stated that criminals target older adults because they hold the majority of wealth in the United States.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that the Justice Department states scammers target older Americans an average of nine times, while The Daily Caller does not mention this figure. FOX News also cites a November 2026 U.S. Secret Service public advisory and includes quotes from USSS Investigative Analyst Bre Whalen and AARP's Amy Nofziger. The Daily Caller includes a survey by Javelin Strategy and quotes Lucas Olson, a fraud analyst, about agentic AI and consumer liability. FOX News mentions a 2025 FTC report with figures on fraud losses, while The Daily Caller cites a 2025 FTC report with different figures on losses and fraud reports.

Sources FOX News · The Daily Caller

No source labeled center or lean-left or lean-right or left covered this story.

Storms across US disrupt travel and force Thanksgiving parade cancellations

A severe winter storm brought heavy rain, winds, flooding and high tides across the US on Thanksgiving, prompting the cancellations of at least two commercial Thanksgiving parades. The storm caused widespread power outages, with more than 900,000 homes and businesses without electricity on Thursday afternoon. In New York, the traditional Macy’s parade was postponed to Saturday for the first time in its history, while Philadelphia’s parade was moved to an “alternative TV event.” The storm also led to coastal flooding, road closures and emergency rescues in several states, including New Jersey and Virginia.

The storm affected air travel at eastern US airports, with delays expected to last into Friday morning. In Florida, President Donald Trump was joined by state leaders to sign a major disaster declaration for the state, which makes federal assistance available to those affected by severe storms and flooding. The National Weather Service reported high tide records in several California cities, including Los Angeles and Santa Barbara, while winter storm warnings were posted for parts of Missouri and Illinois.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both report that more than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday afternoon, while ABC News states that more than 925,000 utility customers in nine states were without power. The Guardian and CBS News also note that the Macy’s parade was postponed to Saturday, while ABC News and The Hill mention that the parade was postponed due to severe weather. The Guardian and CBS News report that the storm caused flooding in coastal villages and cities from North Carolina through New Jersey, while The Hill and ABC News mention that the storm disrupted travel in the Washington, D.C., area. The Guardian and CBS News also report that the storm caused power outages in the Midwest, while The Hill and ABC News mention that the storm knocked out power for more than 850,000 utility customers nationwide.

Sources The Guardian · ABC News · CBS News · Axios · BBC · The Hill

GOP lawmakers warn Trump made himself a target in Nvidia scandal

President Donald Trump’s intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s chief executive is drawing mounting criticism from Republicans, who are questioning whether the president put the company’s financial interests ahead of national security. Republican lawmakers are demanding answers about the Trump administration’s role in Huang’s reinstatement following revelations of his affair with tech executive Alice Huang, who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Of particular concern are reports that Trump and members of his orbit assured Nvidia’s board that Huang posed no national security risk, raising questions about who provided those assurances and what evidence they relied upon.

Nvidia said it received assurances from senior officials that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk. But federal investigations were still underway into the Nvidia CEO's affair with a woman whose alleged ties to Chinese intelligence remain in dispute, as well as questions about advanced U.S. chips reaching China when the president began his push. The decision to reinstate Huang has left Republican lawmakers demanding to know what senior administration officials told Nvidia’s board that led them to reverse course less than two weeks after Huang's resignation.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both report that Trump and members of his orbit assured Nvidia’s board that Huang posed no national security risk, but the Washington Examiner notes that these assurances raised questions about who provided them and what evidence was used. The Guardian adds that the Department of Justice has not confirmed whether a formal investigation was conducted into Huang. The Fox News and Fox Business accounts differ in that Fox News states that Attorney General Todd Blanche assured Vice President JD Vance that Huang was not under investigation, while Fox Business reports that Trump said he had not spoken with Huang since his reinstatement. The The Hill and The Guardian both mention that Trump did not rule out pardoning Huang, but The Guardian adds that JD Vance stated Huang did not need a pardon as he was never under criminal investigation.

Sources Washington Examiner · FOX News · Fox Business · The Hill · The Guardian · NPR

Trump calls for investigation into Commerce Department’s revised GDP figures

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis revised its third quarter GDP report on Wednesday, increasing the annualized growth rate from 3.4% to 4.3%. President Trump responded by demanding an investigation, accusing the department of making a “massive and purposeful” error. The revision came after the November midterm elections, which saw significant losses for Republicans. Trump claimed the initial figures were “FAKE” and that the correct number was not released before the election.

Fox Business reported that the revised GDP figure of 4.3% exceeded economists’ expectations of 3.5% for the quarter. The revision was attributed to higher investment and consumer spending, particularly in software and pharmaceuticals. The report also noted that the upward revision was larger than usual, with the BEA citing updated data on software prices and retail sales as key factors.

Axios highlighted that the initial GDP figure of 3.4% already indicated a strong economy, and the upward revision simply made that picture more favorable. The article also noted that the Commerce Department and BEA did not respond to requests for comment. The revision could bolster the case for further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, which Trump opposes.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and Axios both state that Trump accused the Commerce Department of making a “massive and purposeful” error, while Fox Business does not mention Trump’s accusation of a “purposeful” error. The New York Post and The Guardian attribute Trump’s claim that the figures were “FAKE” to his statements, while CBS News and Axios note that Trump did not provide evidence for his allegations. The Guardian and CBS News include additional context about Trump’s Thanksgiving message and his broader grievances, which are not present in the other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · Fox Business · Axios · The Guardian · CBS News · New York Post

Accused MS-13 Gangbanger Kilmar Abrego Garcia Lands In Spain After Self-Deporting

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national accused of gang activity and human smuggling, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after self-deporting from the United States. He was seen boarding a flight to Madrid from Dulles Airport on Tuesday after having his ankle monitor removed. Garcia, who is married to an American citizen and has a U.S. citizen child, has been fighting deportation for over two years. His attorney, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, stated that Garcia left the U.S. as a "free man" and plans to return in the future. Federal law bars him from re-entering the U.S. for 10 years due to his long-term presence without legal status.

Garcia’s case became a focal point of the Trump administration’s deportation efforts after he was mistakenly deported to El Salvador in 2025. He was initially sent to a notorious prison in El Salvador before being returned to the U.S. after a court order. He was later charged with human smuggling, which was dismissed in 2026 due to concerns about vindictive prosecution. The Justice Department appealed the ruling, and arguments were scheduled for February 2027. Garcia’s lawyer described his departure as temporary, with plans to stay abroad for two years before potentially returning to the U.S.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that Garcia arrived in Spain after leaving the U.S. of his own volition and that he was met by ICE agents at the airport, with his ankle monitor removed. The Federalist adds that Garcia was a "known member" of MS-13 and was in possession of drugs and money during his arrest. The Federalist also claims he was accused of being a "child predator" and of domestic violence, including allegations of bruising, punching, and scratching his wife. The Daily Wire and The Guardian both mention that Garcia’s wife has sponsored him for legal residency, while The Federalist attributes these claims to DHS. The NPR account omits details about Garcia’s alleged crimes and focuses more on the legal battle and his family status.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Guardian · The Federalist · NPR

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump administration approves Elon Musk’s plan for datacenters in space

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved SpaceX’s plan to deploy 1 million satellites to create data centers in space, calling it a step toward a "Kardashev II civilization." The authorization, announced on Wednesday, allows SpaceX to begin deploying satellites no later than November 2033, with 10% deployed by November 2035 and 50% by November 2038. The FCC stated that the project would "support America’s booming super intelligence economy" and "bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun." SpaceX argued that space-based data centers would reduce environmental impact and energy costs compared to terrestrial ones.

Critics, including scientists and industry experts, have raised concerns about the feasibility and risks of such a project. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) warned of "engineering and economic barriers to deployment," noting that space does not cool computing hardware efficiently and that a large number of satellites could lead to collisions. The American Astronomical Society (AAS) criticized the plan for potentially undermining astronomical research and polluting the night sky with bright satellites.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Fox Business both mention that SpaceX sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before deployment, but the Guardian notes that the current network has just over 11,000 satellites in space, while Fox Business states that the growing network currently has just over 11,000 satellites in space. The Guardian also states that it was unclear whether SpaceX would deploy 1 million satellites, while Fox Business mentions that it was unclear whether SpaceX would put 1 million satellites in space. The Guardian and BBC both note that the FCC did not specify whether SpaceX is required to launch all 1 million satellites, while Newsweek states that the authorization does not specify if SpaceX is required to launch all 1 million satellites.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · Newsweek · BBC · Fox Business

No source labeled right covered this story.

Trump celebrates Thanksgiving with his holiday tradition of hate-posting against his enemies — including far left, sharia backers

President Trump used his Thanksgiving message on Truth Social to criticize a range of groups, including the "Radical Far Left," the Somali-American community, and the New York Times. He praised a small percentage of the Somali population for working without government assistance, while calling for the rest to be deported. Trump also criticized the Bureau of Economic Analysis for revising GDP numbers upward after the midterms, calling the adjustment a "massive, and purposeful, error." He claimed the revision showed the economy was stronger than previously reported, which he said was "fake" before the election. In addition, Trump took aim at a New York Times journalist, David Sanger, for not highlighting his economic achievements in a recent article. He accused Sanger of being a "lowlife" who only writes what he is told by his bosses.

Melania Trump, meanwhile, directed her Thanksgiving message to American troops, expressing gratitude for their service. She wrote, "May god bless our nation and protect our troops," on social media. Trump also highlighted his accomplishments on border security and tax cuts, claiming they contributed to the improved economic conditions.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and The Daily Wire both mention Trump’s criticism of the New York Times and David Sanger, with the New York Post including specific details about the article and Trump’s accusation that Sanger only writes what he is told. The Washington Examiner omits any mention of the Times or Sanger, focusing instead on Trump’s general Thanksgiving message. The FOX News account includes more specific details about Trump’s comments on the Somali community, including his call to deport those receiving government assistance. The New York Post also includes a separate article about Abdul El-Sayed’s Thanksgiving message, which is not covered by the other outlets.

Sources New York Post · Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Ebola outbreak surpassing 12,000 cases in DR Congo disrupts healthcare and threatens communities amid conflict, risking widespread health crises.

DR Congo Ebola cases surpass 12,000 as fighting disrupts response in east

The number of confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has surpassed 12,000, according to government data, as escalating fighting in the east disrupts efforts to contain the country’s deadliest outbreak on record. Health officials and humanitarian workers reported that Ebola response workers have been forced to leave affected areas amid worsening violence in the eastern DRC. The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus, was declared in mid-May in Ituri province in the northeastern DRC. There are no approved treatments or vaccines for this species.

Fighting between the Congolese army and fighters from the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) has intensified in recent days, displacing civilians, according to the United Nations mission. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization’s Ebola incident manager, said about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia after three days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire. The CRP is led by Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of conscripting child soldiers. The group declared a unilateral ceasefire in May, but fighting has continued.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that at least 12,021 infections have been confirmed, including 5,904 deaths, while NPR states that nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died. Al Jazeera does not mention the death toll percentage, while NPR provides it. NPR also states that the outbreak is the fastest-growing in history and on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016, a claim not made by Al Jazeera. Al Jazeera notes that the outbreak is the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks, a detail not included in NPR's account.

Sources Al Jazeera · NPR

No source labeled lean-right or left or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Iowa braces for controlled bomb blast: ‘We had only five days of warning’

The U.S. Army has scheduled a controlled detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Wednesday. The operation, delayed multiple times due to public outcry and legal challenges, is now set for 10 a.m. EST. Officials claim the detonation is the only viable option to prevent an uncontrolled explosion of the unstable material, which was discovered to be dangerously unstable earlier this year. The blast is expected to release toxic chemicals in a 100-mile radius, with residents within five miles advised to evacuate and those within 20 miles told to stay indoors. The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services recommends staying indoors for 24-48 hours after the blast, conflicting with the timing of Thanksgiving, a major travel day.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Mother Jones both mention that the initial public announcement was made on 15 November, five days before the initially scheduled detonation, but The Guardian notes that neighboring communities were not informed until the army publicly announced plans on 15 November. Mother Jones states that the initial public announcement was made on 15 November, five days before the initially scheduled detonation, but does not specify that neighboring communities were not informed until then. The Hill and CBS News both mention that the detonation was initially planned for last Friday but was rescheduled three times, while The Guardian and Mother Jones also note the rescheduling but do not specify the exact number of times. The Guardian and CBS News both mention that the detonation is scheduled for Wednesday, but CBS News specifies the time as 9 a.m. and the date as the day before Thanksgiving, while The Guardian does not specify the exact time or date.

Sources The Guardian · Mother Jones · ABC News · CBS News · Newsweek · The Hill

Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed for first time in history

The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, marking its 100th anniversary, has been postponed for the first time in its history due to severe weather. The event, which typically takes place on Thanksgiving Day, will now occur on Saturday at 8:30 a.m. The decision was made after consultations with city and agency officials, citing safety concerns related to an approaching storm. Macy's stated that the safety of participants and spectators is their top priority. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani acknowledged the inconvenience but emphasized that safety must come first. The National Weather Service has issued high wind warnings, with gusts potentially reaching 60 mph, which could make it unsafe for the balloons to fly.

The parade, which features giant inflatables and live performances, has been a New York tradition since 1924. This year's event was expected to include 100 inflatables, including new designs. The balloons are typically inflated on the Upper West Side, but due to the storm, they will be deflated and stored in New Jersey until Saturday. The NYPD has confirmed that there are no known specific or credible threats to the parade, though an increased police presence will be on hand for security.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that the storm is a "powerful coastal storm" with wind gusts up to 65 mph, while ABC News states the forecast calls for gusts up to 40 mph. Axios mentions wind gusts up to 55 mph, and BBC reports gusts potentially reaching 60 mph. The Daily Wire and Newsweek both cite the National Weather Service's warning about wind gusts exceeding 60 mph. CBS News and ABC News differ in the number of times the parade has been postponed, with CBS stating it's the first time and ABC noting it was only canceled three times during World War II. The Daily Wire also mentions the parade was canceled from 1942 through 1944, which is consistent with other accounts. Newsweek adds that Mayor Mamdani will miss the rescheduled parade due to a scheduled surgery, a detail not included in other accounts.

Sources CBS News · Axios · ABC News · BBC · The Daily Wire · Newsweek

FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing brief suspension of flights at airport

A FedEx aircraft overshot a runway at Miami International Airport on Wednesday evening, prompting the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to issue a ground stop. The incident occurred around 8:40 p.m., according to multiple outlets, and led to the closure of all but one runway at the airport. Flights resumed approximately 90 minutes later, though delays persisted into Thursday morning. No injuries were reported, and the FAA is investigating the cause. The event took place on Thanksgiving Eve, one of the busiest travel days of the year.

The FAA confirmed that flights would be resuming shortly after the incident, though some sources noted that the ground stop remained in effect for several hours. The airport advised passengers to check directly with their airlines for the latest updates. The incident occurred near the site of a previous runway overrun in September, where a Prime Air cargo jet crashed into a road, killing five people.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that the FAA temporarily halted flights bound for Miami International Airport just after 20:15 local time, while New York Post and FOX News state the ground stop was issued around 8:40 p.m. Washington Examiner mentions the ground stop was issued at 8:16 p.m. EST, and ABC News states the incident happened around 8:40 p.m. The New York Post and FOX News attribute the incident to a FedEx cargo plane veering off the runway, while BBC and ABC News refer to it as an airliner that ran past the runway. ABC News also notes that the FedEx plane landed on a different runway than the one involved in the September incident, while FOX News and Just The News mention the FedEx plane ran off Runway 26R.

Sources BBC · New York Post · Washington Examiner · FOX News · ABC News · Just The News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Judge criticizes Trump administration for weaponizing law enforcement in Hunter Biden probe

A federal judge has issued a scathing rebuke of the Trump administration for what he called the "weaponization" of federal law enforcement in the Hunter Biden probe. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui dismissed a criminal case against two former FBI agents, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, for allegedly lying to Congress about their involvement in the investigation. Faruqui criticized the Department of Justice for rushing the prosecution, which he said was motivated by political pressure from the White House. The judge also highlighted the involvement of FBI Director Kash Patel, who assigned the case to the FBI's Kansas City office after President Trump directed the agency to investigate any slights related to the 2020 election.

In a separate ruling, a federal judge blocked the Federal Communications Commission from proceeding with an early review of ABC's broadcast licenses, calling the move an unconstitutional retaliation for the network's speech. U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan found that the FCC's actions were motivated by President Trump's public calls for the agency to strip ABC of its licenses. The judge ruled that the early review created a chilling effect on free speech and that the FCC had weaponized its licensing authority to retaliate against broadcasters for their editorial decisions.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News reports that Judge Faruqui criticized the Trump administration for weaponizing law enforcement in the Hunter Biden probe, calling it a "slapdash prosecution" in response to a public command from the President. Newsweek, however, reports that the judge blocked the FCC from reviewing ABC's licenses and called the move an unconstitutional retaliation for the network's speech. NPR and CBS News also describe the same ruling, but NPR adds that the judge cited specific examples of Trump's public calls for stripping ABC's licenses, including one in July 2026. Washington Examiner and Newsweek both mention the judge's decision to block the FCC review, but only Newsweek provides details about the judge's reasoning and the specific examples of Trump's rhetoric.

Sources ABC News · Newsweek · NPR · CBS News · Washington Examiner

No source labeled left or right covered this story.

US preparing to unveil plan for new tariffs on global trading partners

The US administration has proposed new tariffs on imports from 14 major trading partners, including China, the European Union, and several Asian countries. The tariffs are being introduced under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, following a legal challenge to previous tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The proposed duties aim to address what the administration calls unfair foreign manufacturing practices that disadvantage American producers. The tariffs are not expected to take effect until next year and will undergo public consultation and hearings before finalization.

The new tariffs are part of a broader trade policy that includes investigations into the trade practices of various countries. The administration argues that foreign governments have supported domestic manufacturing through subsidies and other policies that drive down prices and weaken American industries. The proposed tariffs vary by country, with China facing up to 20% in some cases, which could be stacked with existing tariffs to reach 40%. Other countries, such as Vietnam, face up to 35%, while the EU, Japan, and South Korea face up to 15% or 18%. The administration claims the tariffs are based on trade agreements and investigations, and they are not automatically stacked on top of existing duties.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that the new tariffs will not take effect until next year and will go through rounds of public consultation and hearings. The Daily Wire states that a public hearing is scheduled to begin January 25, 2027, and no effective date has been announced. The Guardian mentions that the tariffs could go into effect as early as January, with hearings on January 25. Fox Business notes that the review and hearing process for the broader overcapacity duties could push final implementation into January. Axios states that the levies could take effect as early as January.

Sources BBC · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · Fox Business · Axios

Aaron Rodgers released by Steelers after public clash with coach Mike McCarthy

Aaron Rodgers was released by the Pittsburgh Steelers on Wednesday after a public fallout with head coach Mike McCarthy. Rodgers, a four-time NFL Most Valuable Player, was benched as the starting quarterback on Tuesday and did not return to the team. During an appearance on the Pat McAfee Show, Rodgers accused McCarthy of sleeping during meetings and missing key team gatherings. McCarthy admitted to an "embarrassing moment" when he broke a halftime huddle with "1-2-3 Packers" during a loss to the Eagles. The Steelers confirmed Rodgers' release in a brief statement, ending his two-year stint with the team.

Rodgers claimed he discovered his benching during a phone call with teammate Pat Freiermuth, who informed him of the decision. He criticized McCarthy for failing to engage with defensive players and for not keeping up with film study. McCarthy stated that Rodgers had presented an "ultimatum" that was outside his job description, leading to the release. The Steelers named Mason Rudolph as the new starter for Friday's game against the Broncos.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that McCarthy admitted to the "embarrassing moment" during a press conference, while The Guardian states McCarthy admitted to the "Packers" mishap during his own news conference. The Daily Wire and The Guardian mention that Rodgers claimed McCarthy told a Steelers staffer he blamed Rodgers for his firing by the Packers in 2018, a claim not included in BBC, NPR, or Newsweek. NPR and The Guardian note that Rodgers said he learned of his benching from Freiermuth, while BBC and Newsweek state Rodgers was informed during a phone call with Freiermuth. The Daily Wire and The Guardian mention that Rodgers said McCarthy had watched only clips of game film three days before a game, a detail not in BBC, NPR, or Newsweek.

Sources BBC · NPR · Newsweek · The Daily Wire · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Melania Trump reunites seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children with families

First Lady Melania Trump has helped return a seventh group of Ukrainian and Russian children to their families, bringing the total number of children in these reunifications to 43, according to the White House. The first lady said the reunification of nine children with their families took place with the “full cooperation” of Russian and Ukrainian leaders. She has made helping children in conflict zones a key focus of her efforts, including hosting a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year. Her work began in August 2025, when she had President Donald Trump hand-deliver a letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin during a summit in Alaska, calling for peace in Ukraine.

Melania Trump’s efforts have included securing a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, which allowed for the evacuation of 800 people and the delivery of humanitarian aid. The ceasefire, which was in effect from October 27 to November 1, marked a significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The first lady also hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House to mark the milestone, crediting both leaders for their cooperation.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and The Daily Wire both state that Melania Trump helped reunite nine children with their families, marking the seventh group, and that the total number of children reunified is 43. Just The News and New York Post also report the same numbers. However, New York Post mentions that Russia is estimated to have kidnapped more than 35,000 children from Ukraine since the start of the war, a figure not included in the other accounts. Additionally, New York Post notes that the Humanitarian Research Lab at Yale provided the estimate of 35,000 children kidnapped, while the other accounts do not mention this statistic. The Daily Wire and Just The News attribute the statement about the ceasefire in Oleshky and the impact on 800 people to the White House, while New York Post attributes it to the first lady’s office.

Sources ABC News · The Daily Wire · Just The News · New York Post

No source labeled left covered this story.

Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering

Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but acquitted of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice. The case, which spanned a two-month trial in Brooklyn, involved allegations that Huawei engaged in deceptive practices to gain a competitive edge. Prosecutors claimed Huawei lied to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stole technology from American companies. Huawei's defense argued that the case was built on the assumption that the company was a criminal organization, and that its success was due to innovation and hard work. The verdict follows a long-standing legal battle that began in 2019, after the arrest of Huawei's CFO, Meng Wanzhou, in Canada.

The convictions could result in significant financial penalties for Huawei, though the company has stated it will appeal. Huawei's defense attorney, Brian Heberlig, called the racketeering acquittal a "profound rejection" of the U.S. narrative about the company. He argued that the prosecution cherry-picked incidents to build a 20-year conspiracy. The case did not involve individual defendants, though Meng Wanzhou was previously charged with misleading HSBC about Huawei's Iran business.

Where the accounts differ

BBC and The Daily Caller both state Huawei was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy, but The Daily Caller adds that Huawei was also acquitted of conspiracy to obstruct justice. The Daily Wire and Fox Business mention the acquittal of conspiracy to obstruct justice, while The Daily Wire also specifies that the convictions included stealing T-Mobile’s testing robot technology. Fox Business and The Daily Wire include details about the role of Skycom, a subsidiary used to conduct business in Iran, which The Daily Caller omits. The Daily Wire and Fox Business name specific U.S. companies whose trade secrets were allegedly stolen, including Cisco, T-Mobile, and Quintel, while BBC and The Daily Caller do not specify these companies. The Daily Wire and Fox Business mention the role of the U.S. Attorney General in the case, while BBC and The Daily Caller attribute statements to the U.S. Attorney General differently.

Sources BBC · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · Fox Business

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

Gaza issues meningitis epidemic alert after steep rise in cases

The Gaza health ministry has issued an epidemic alert due to a sharp rise in meningitis infections, with over 270 new cases reported in October. Dr. Nidal Ghoneim, a senior official at the ministry, stated that the spread of the disease poses a threat to hundreds of thousands of people, including children. Health organizations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters, and contaminated drinking water, exacerbated by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid. The UN’s humanitarian agency (OCHA) previously reported 413 suspected cases of meningitis in Gaza between September 27 and October 31, including 294 viral and 119 bacterial cases. About 68% were recorded in Gaza City. The World Health Organization noted that microbial contamination in water samples had risen from less than 6% in January to nearly 20% in August.

A five-year-old boy, Omar Abu Fayed, has been admitted to the isolation ward at Gaza City’s Rantisi Children’s Hospital multiple times for meningitis. His mother, Zakia Abu Fayed, reported that Omar’s symptoms returned after each discharge, leading to repeated hospitalizations. She believes Omar may have contracted the infection at kindergarten, though the source remains undetermined. The ministry reported 272 cases in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate of 30 to 50 cases. It also noted 15 deaths from meningitis since the beginning of 2026, including five between August and October. The ministry attributed the epidemic outbreak to the Israeli occupation’s prevention of essential supplies.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports 272 meningitis infections in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate of 30 to 50 cases, and 15 deaths since the beginning of this year. Al Jazeera states that the ministry reported 15 deaths from the disease since the beginning of 2026, including five between August and October. The Guardian attributes the epidemic outbreak to the Israeli occupation’s prevention of essential supplies, while Al Jazeera does not mention this attribution. The Guardian also reports that the UN’s OCHA had previously reported 413 suspected cases of meningitis in Gaza between September 27 and October 31, including 294 viral and 119 bacterial cases, while Al Jazeera does not include these specific numbers.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera

US Army to detonate 68 barrels of lead azide in Iowa amid legal and political delays

The US Army has announced it will proceed with a controlled detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, scheduled for Wednesday morning. The operation, delayed multiple times due to public outcry and legal challenges, involves the destruction of a stockpile of degraded lead azide, a highly volatile chemical used in munitions. The Army claims the material, stored for over two decades, has recrystallized and poses a significant risk of spontaneous detonation if moved. Officials say the detonation is the only viable option to prevent a more dangerous uncontrolled explosion.

The detonation is expected to release a plume of toxic lead dust over a 100-mile radius, with the exact path of the plume changing with each rescheduling. Residents within five miles are advised to evacuate, and those within 20 miles are told to stay indoors with windows closed. The Iowa Department of Health recommends staying indoors for 24-48 hours after the blast, conflicting with the timing of Thanksgiving, a major travel day. The Army has implemented mitigation measures, including installing a dam and using aqueous foam to absorb lead, following public pressure and court rulings.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both mention that the detonation was initially scheduled for last Friday but was rescheduled three times, while the BBC and Axios state the initial date was Friday and the plan was delayed to Monday and then to Wednesday. The Guardian and Mother Jones note that the Army initially planned the detonation for last Friday, but the BBC and Axios say the initial date was Friday and the plan was delayed to Monday and then to Wednesday. The Guardian and CBS News report that the Army moved the detonation to Wednesday to allow for optimal weather conditions and safety measures, while the BBC and Axios state the Army delayed the detonation to Wednesday to allow for optimal weather conditions and safety measures. The Guardian and CBS News mention that the Army has implemented mitigation measures, including installing a dam and using aqueous foam to absorb lead, following public pressure and court rulings, while the BBC and Axios state that the Army has implemented mitigation measures, including installing a dam and using aqueous foam to absorb lead, following public pressure and court rulings.

Sources The Guardian · Mother Jones · Al Jazeera · CBS News · Axios · BBC

Kilmar Ábrego García leaves US for Spain, ending Trump deportation battle

Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national, left the United States for Spain on Tuesday. He departed on a commercial flight, ending a prolonged legal battle with the Trump administration. García was initially deported to El Salvador in March 2025 despite a 2019 court order barring his removal due to gang-related risks. The administration later admitted the deportation was an error and brought him back to the U.S., where he faced human trafficking charges that were later dismissed. The Trump administration continued efforts to deport him to other countries, including Uganda, Ghana, and Liberia. García had previously expressed willingness to be deported to Costa Rica, which agreed to accept him as a refugee. His departure marks the end of a 20-month legal struggle.

García, who is married to a U.S. citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the U.S. illegally from El Salvador as a teenager. His case was elevated to the Supreme Court, which ordered the government to facilitate his return. Federal prosecutors had alleged he transported hundreds of illegal migrants, but the case was dismissed by a federal judge in May 2026. García’s legal team stated his departure was "temporary" and that he had "many options to return to the United States," though they expect the next administration to prioritize his family reunification.

Where the accounts differ

BBC and Al Jazeera both report that García was held in El Salvador’s CECOT prison, while FOX News and The Daily Wire describe the facility as a "terrorism confinement center." The Daily Wire and The Washington Examiner mention that García was arrested in 2019 and granted protection from deportation to El Salvador, a detail not included in the BBC or Al Jazeera accounts. The Washington Examiner and Just The News state that García voluntarily left the U.S. for Spain, while FOX News and The Daily Wire describe his departure as following a removal order. The Daily Wire and The Washington Examiner note that García was charged with human smuggling in Tennessee, a detail omitted by the BBC and Al Jazeera. The BBC and The Daily Wire mention that García’s lawyer stated his departure was "temporary," while FOX News and The Washington Examiner do not include this statement.

Sources BBC · Washington Examiner · Just The News · Al Jazeera · FOX News · The Daily Wire

Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia. And, Rep. Gomez resigns amid alleged sexual misconduct

Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, leading to a more than 30% surge in its stock. Huang's return followed his resignation two weeks earlier due to reports of extramarital affairs, including alleged involvement with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Trump claimed credit for facilitating Huang's return. The stock rally highlights the significant impact of Huang's reinstatement on the market. Meanwhile, Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., announced his resignation from Congress after a House ethics report found "substantial evidence" of his alleged sexual misconduct toward a House staffer. The report detailed "unwelcome sexual advances" and "sexual contact" by Gomez, which caused the staffer "significant and ongoing distress."

The House Ethics Committee report on Gomez found that he made "unwelcome sexual advances" toward a House staffer, disregarding the power imbalance. The report also noted that Gomez's conduct reflects a broader environment of sexual misconduct in some Capitol Hill offices. Gomez, who lost his re-election bid, said he had "strong disagreements" with the report but acknowledged "personal mistakes" outside his marriage. The report did not make specific recommendations for sanctions against Gomez, as he was set to leave Congress.

Where the accounts differ

NPR mentions that Trump claimed credit for facilitating Huang's return and that Huang had previously donated $25 million to the new White House ballroom and security complex. The Guardian and BBC do not mention Trump's claim or the donation. The Guardian and BBC provide more detail on the nature of the sexual misconduct allegations, including specific incidents and the role of the House Ethics Committee. FOX News states that the report warned Gomez could have violated existing law, including D.C. laws related to criminal sexual assault, which the other accounts do not explicitly mention. The New York Post and The Daily Wire describe the allegations as "credible" and "substantial evidence" of sexual assault, while the Guardian and BBC use similar language but do not specify the nature of the alleged assault beyond "sexual contact" and "unwelcome sexual advances."

Sources NPR · The Guardian · BBC · FOX News · New York Post · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump pardons turkeys Freedom and Feathers during 2026 National Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon

President Donald Trump pardoned two turkeys, Freedom and Feathers, during the 2026 National Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon. The ceremony took place on the South Lawn of the White House, where Trump delivered remarks about the event. The turkeys were raised on a farm in Fort Seybert, West Virginia, and their names were selected through a White House public poll. Both turkeys will be sent to Texas A&M University for retirement. The event is part of an annual tradition that dates back to 1947, with the formal pardon tradition beginning in 1989 under President George H.W. Bush.

The National Turkey Federation, which has been involved in the tradition since 1947, stated that the turkeys were named through a public vote, with Freedom and Feathers beating out other options like "Commander and Chief" and "Honey and Ham." The turkeys spent Monday night at the Willard InterContinental Hotel in Washington, D.C., where they were provided with special accommodations, including a premium room with two queen beds and tailored room service. The turkeys will be cared for by students at Texas A&M University.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire both mention that the ceremony took place on the South Lawn, while FOX News and The Guardian note that it was held on the new South Lawn helipad. The Guardian and The Daily Wire describe the turkeys as arriving at the Willard InterContinental Hotel, while the Washington Examiner does not specify the location of the turkeys prior to the ceremony. The Guardian and The Daily Wire also mention that the turkeys stayed overnight at the hotel, a detail not included in the Washington Examiner or Newsweek accounts. The Guardian and The Daily Wire attribute the comment about Trump winning West Virginia by a large margin to Scott Rightsell, while the Washington Examiner and FOX News attribute it to Trump himself.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · Newsweek · Axios · FOX News · The Guardian

All 6 passengers found dead inside wreckage of plane off Mississippi coast

A small plane crashed off the Mississippi Gulf Coast on Tuesday, resulting in the deaths of all six people on board. Divers located the remains of the victims inside the aircraft's fuselage approximately 2 miles northeast of Horn Island, Mississippi, according to the U.S. Coast Guard. The victims included four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10. The Cessna 210 was traveling from New Orleans Lakefront Airport to Page Field in Fort Myers, Florida, when it crashed. The plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute when contact was lost, as reported by multiple outlets. Rescue crews initially found debris including a life raft and three life jackets, but the bodies were not recovered until later. The FAA and NTSB are conducting an investigation into the crash.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that the victims' identities have not been released, while CBS News, The Guardian, and BBC all state that the victims included two children, aged 8 and 10. Just The News does not specify the ages of the children but confirms there were two boys. CBS News and BBC mention the FAA confirmed the crash location as southwest of Pascagoula, Mississippi, at about 3:30 p.m. local time, while FOX News states the FAA confirmed the crash occurred southwest of Pascagoula at about 3:30 p.m. local time. The Guardian and BBC attribute the statement about the plane descending at 10,000 feet per minute to the Coast Guard, while FOX News and CBS News attribute it to the Coast Guard and FAA respectively.

Sources FOX News · CBS News · Just The News · The Guardian · BBC

Pope Francis had visions of devil, "gates of hell," diary reveals

Pope Francis described experiencing visions of the devil and seeing the "gates of hell" in his private diary, according to excerpts published by the Vatican. The diary, spanning from 1992 to 2024, includes accounts of spiritual struggles, including a profound crisis in 2021-2022. The diary was curated by Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, who is listed as the author. The book details Francis' encounters with the devil, including three specific instances: one from a car, another in a choir loft during Mass, and a third during a meeting in Rome. The diary also reflects on his 2018 trip to Chile, where he faced criticism for defending a bishop accused of covering up sexual abuse, leading to a spiritual reckoning.

Francis wrote about feeling "devastated" by the Chile scandal and described seeing the entrance to hell, which he associated with "pagan seduction in full force." He expressed gratitude to God for helping him overcome these experiences. The diary also mentions his struggle with temptations to wield power and his eventual reliance on God's mercy to navigate these challenges.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and The Daily Wire both mention that Francis described seeing the devil three times, with specific locations: from a car, in a choir loft during Mass, and during a meeting in Rome. The Daily Caller and The Daily Wire also note that Francis described the devil's voice as "triumphant, possessing everything," while CBS News and The Daily Wire include the exact quote: "Now I've gotten everything I wanted." FOX News and The Daily Wire both mention that Francis saw the entrance to hell in June 2018, but FOX News adds that he "peeked in to look a little, and it terrified me. I grabbed the Rosary as a weapon." The Daily Wire and CBS News attribute the description of the devil's eyes as "menacing" to Francis, while The Daily Caller and The Daily Wire describe them as "seductive."

Sources CBS News · BBC · Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller

No source labeled left covered this story.

Intruders Spark Drone And Helicopter Response At British Royal Residence

Police responded Monday to a break-in at the country home of Prince William and Kate Middleton. Two men were arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespass. The property was unoccupied at the time of the incident. Specialist resources, including police dogs, drones, and a helicopter, were deployed to assist with searches. Kensington Palace stated the family was at their main home in Windsor Great Park during the incident. Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom home, was a wedding gift from Queen Elizabeth II in 2011. The Prince of Wales’ main residence is Forest Lodge in Windsor.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and CBS News both report that Prince William and Kate were not present at Anmer Hall during the incident. The Daily Caller states that the family was in London at the time. CBS News mentions that Prince William was visiting Prime Minister Andy Burnham at 10 Downing Street during the incident, a detail not included in the other accounts. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller note that the property was unoccupied, while CBS News does not specify whether the property was occupied or not. The Daily Wire provides additional historical context about previous break-ins at royal properties, which the other accounts do not include.

Sources The Daily Wire · CBS News · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan seeks stay of execution to challenge death sentence

Nidal Hasan, the former U.S. Army officer convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, has filed a motion in civilian court to halt his execution. The motion, supported by the American Civil Liberties Union, seeks a stay so Hasan can file a habeas corpus petition challenging the constitutionality of his death sentence. Hasan is scheduled to be executed by an Army firing squad on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, Texas. The execution would be the first military death sentence carried out in over six decades.

Hasan, who was convicted in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder, remains on military death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. His legal team argues that he must have the opportunity to pursue federal review of his case. The Army has also denied the request of three survivors of the 2009 shooting to witness the execution, citing regulations that define direct victims as those who were physically wounded by gunfire.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News and The Guardian both report that Hasan sought a stay of execution, but only FOX News attributes the claim to Hasan himself. The Guardian and ABC News mention that the Army denied the request of three survivors to witness the execution, but only The Guardian and ABC News specify that the survivors were not physically wounded by gunfire. CBS News and The Washington Examiner also mention the denial of the survivors’ request, but only CBS News and The Guardian provide the names of the survivors. The Guardian and ABC News include quotes from retired Colonel Kathy Platoni about the denial feeling like a betrayal, while FOX News and CBS News also include similar quotes but attribute them to different sources.

Sources FOX News · The Guardian · ABC News · CBS News · Washington Examiner · Just The News

No source labeled center covered this story.
