Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO After Board Reversal

Nvidia's board of directors reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO effective immediately following a reversal of its earlier decision to remove him. Huang had resigned earlier this month amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving Alice Huang, a woman identified by U.S. intelligence as a possible Chinese government spy. The board cited satisfaction with Huang's candor and leadership ability, and stated it received input from senior U.S. government officials that confirmed no national security risk. Nvidia stock surged over 30% following the announcement, with broader markets also seeing significant gains. The decision has drawn mixed reactions, with some praising it as necessary for the company's future and others expressing concerns about national security implications.

Where the accounts differ

Fox Business reports that the board received input from senior U.S. government officials and that the decision was influenced by the U.S. government's assessment of Huang's national security risk. Mother Jones states that the board received input from senior U.S. government officials and that President Trump spoke directly with the board, reassuring them about Huang's safety. Axios and The New York Post note that Trump and Vice President JD Vance worked to reinstate Huang and that the administration viewed Huang's support for open-source AI as a backstop against major AI companies accruing uncontested capabilities. The Daily Wire characterizes the reinstatement as a business move that supports open-source AI models, while Fox News and The New York Post highlight Trump's direct involvement and the administration's security briefings.

Sources Fox Business · Mother Jones · Axios · FOX News · The Daily Wire · New York Post

Trump Blocks Army’s Toxic “Lead Bomb”—And Blames Rob Sand For the Fallout

The U.S. Army planned to detonate 68 barrels of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a hazardous material that has degraded over 20 years. The detonation, initially scheduled for Friday, was postponed multiple times due to public concern and legal challenges. President Trump announced on Truth Social that he would not proceed with the detonation without approval from the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals and incoming Iowa Governor-elect Rob Sand. The Army stated it would proceed with the detonation on Wednesday to allow for optimal weather conditions and mitigation measures. The Department of Justice warned of an "immediate risk" that the lead azide could explode if temperatures drop below 30 degrees. Residents of Middletown, Iowa, were given just a month’s notice of the plan, with other nearby communities learning of it only five days before the initial planned date.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and The Guardian both state that the Army postponed the detonation to Wednesday, while FOX News and CBS News mention the Army had delayed the plan to Monday before the court stepped in. The Hill reports that the Army postponed the detonation to Wednesday after a court pause, while The Guardian notes the Army changed the date three times. The Daily Wire and The Guardian attribute the delay to weather conditions, while CBS News and FOX News mention the Army’s need to allow for mitigation measures. The Hill and The Guardian note that the Army warned of an "immediate risk" of an uncontrolled explosion, while FOX News and CBS News cite the Department of Justice as the source of that warning. The Daily Wire and The Guardian attribute the existence of the lead azide to the Obama administration, while CBS News and The Guardian do not specify the origin of the material.

Sources Mother Jones · The Hill · FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · CBS News

Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack

A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel. Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government confirmed the strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies. The attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine, marked a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed responsibility for the attack, stating that seven domestically made sea drones were used to sink the ship. The UN mission in Libya expressed “serious concern” over the drone attacks and called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation.”

Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies, the Ascalon, was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion. Libyan naval forces rescued the vessel’s crew, with some members in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known. The eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and BBC both report that the attack occurred in Benghazi, with the Merkury being the Russian warship struck. The Guardian states that at least four drones were intercepted and two hit the ship, while the BBC notes that the health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast of the port, but it is unclear if this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for. CBS News and Al Jazeera both mention that the Merkury was one of Russia’s newest vessels, commissioned in 2023, while the Guardian and BBC do not specify the vessel’s commission date. FOX News does not mention the Merkury by name and instead refers to it as the corvette Mercury, and it focuses more on the political implications of the attack rather than the event itself.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · Al Jazeera · CBS News · BBC · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump announces federal death penalty directive as he blasts Newsom’s clemency plan

President Donald Trump announced Monday that he would direct the Justice Department to seek the death penalty in federal child murder cases and in cases in which rapists or human traffickers kill their victims. He used the speech at the DOJ headquarters to condemn outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom’s (D-CA) plan to commute 548 California death sentences. Trump’s directive would tell federal prosecutors to seek the death penalty in child murder cases and in cases involving rape or human trafficking in which the offender kills the victim. The move would have no effect on Newsom’s plan to replace 548 state death sentences with life without parole, which Trump condemned before an audience that included victims’ families.

Trump said he would sign a presidential directive that would also order federal prosecutors to seek the death penalty for rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims. "Once juries have spoken, capital punishment will be swift and certain," he said. Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he intended to replace all 548 death sentences with life in prison without parole, arguing that capital punishment is incompatible with the state’s values. Trump and several speakers described the commutations as already granted, but the plan has yet to take effect. Under California’s Constitution, 382 of the proposed commutations require a recommendation from the state Supreme Court because the inmates were convicted of more than one felony. Newsom’s administration has said it will wait for the court to act before proceeding with any of the commutations.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and FOX News both report that Trump condemned Newsom’s plan to commute 548 death sentences, but the Examiner notes that Trump’s directive would have no effect on Newsom’s plan, while FOX News states that Trump described the commutations as already granted. The Guardian and Just The News both mention that Newsom’s plan does not release any prisoners, overturn convictions, or remove restitution obligations, but the Guardian adds that most of the commutations require approval from the California Supreme Court. The New York Post and The Daily Wire both include quotes from Marc Klaas, but the Daily Wire attributes the quote "a shiv in my back" to Klaas, while the New York Post attributes it to Klaas as well, but the Guardian and FOX News do not include this specific quote.

Sources Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Just The News · The Guardian · New York Post

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Federal court releases Rep. Ilhan Omar D.C. home raid documents

A federal court released documents related to the search warrant and raid of Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., home. The documents, obtained by multiple outlets, include exchanges between federal prosecutors and a magistrate judge regarding probable cause, constitutional privilege, and the warrant's execution. The search, conducted by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) on October 12, targeted electronic devices and records, including computers, cellphones, and external hard drives. The documents also mention that the warrant was initially sealed due to concerns about evidence tampering and witness intimidation.

The documents reveal that federal officials applied for a search warrant on October 2, seeking records related to alleged violations involving Ilhan Nur Said Elmi a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, spanning from 1980 to the present. Prosecutors argued that the investigation predated Omar's time in Congress, and that the United States believes she has committed "REDACTED" crimes over decades. The search warrant was signed by a judge on October 9, and the warrant was sealed three days before the raid. The U.S. Attorney's Office requested that the files remain confidential for potential use in a future trial.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News states that the U.S. Attorney's Office, Jeanine Pirro, requested that the files not be released, while The Daily Wire and FOX News note that the documents were unsealed following a lawsuit by 15 media outlets and Judicial Watch. The New York Post and Washington Examiner mention that the documents were released under a court order, with the latter noting that the search warrant records were unsealed after a judge's ruling. The Daily Wire and FOX News attribute the claim that the United States believes Omar committed crimes over decades to the federal government's filings, while CBS News and The New York Post also include this claim but attribute it to the government's filings. The Daily Wire and FOX News cite Fox News as the source for the claim about the ex parte brief, while CBS News and The New York Post do not attribute the claim to a specific outlet.

Sources CBS News · The Daily Wire · Just The News · FOX News · Washington Examiner · New York Post

No source labeled left covered this story.

Dems Unveil 2028 Primary Debate Plan And Draw Their First Red Line

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) announced plans to hold 12 presidential primary debates in the 2028 cycle, with five debates scheduled for 2027 and seven for 2028. Candidates must agree to denounce dark money spending and avoid joint fundraising agreements with party committees to qualify for the debate stage. The DNC emphasized the need for a fair and transparent process to ensure unity within the party and strengthen its eventual nominee. The first two debates are set for June and July 2027, with specific criteria for the early debates to be announced in January 2027. The DNC also mentioned that early debates may involve up to 20 candidates, potentially held over two consecutive nights.

The DNC's plan includes a "Fair Campaign Practices Pledge" requiring candidates to denounce dark money spending and coordinate party spending during the primary. The pledge does not apply to the general election. The DNC will use polling and grassroots fundraising to determine eligibility for the debate stage, with the specific criteria for the first two debates to be announced in January 2027. The DNC also highlighted the importance of maintaining party unity and positioning Democrats to take back the White House.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and ABC News both mention that five debates will be held in 2027, with the first two in June and July 2027. However, ABC News specifies that six of the 2028 debates will be in states with early primaries: South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan, and Virginia. The Guardian does not mention specific states for the 2028 debates. The Daily Wire lists potential candidates including Kamala Harris, Gavin Newsom, Jon Ossoff, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Pete Buttigieg, Josh Shapiro, and Mark Kelly, while the Guardian includes JB Pritzker, Andy Beshear, and mentions early polling showing support for younger and more progressive candidates. The Guardian also notes that the DNC will incorporate "creators and influencers" in the process, which the other accounts do not mention.

Sources The Daily Wire · ABC News · Axios · The Guardian · FOX News · Just The News

Video of ICE detaining father and daughter while boarding flight sparks protests in Seattle

A video of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers detaining a father and daughter while they boarded an Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport has sparked widespread protests. The incident, captured on camera by fellow passengers, went viral on social media and drew condemnation from Washington state officials, including Governor Bob Ferguson and Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson. Protesters gathered at the airport, chanting slogans such as “ICE out of Washington” and “Abolish ICE.” The father, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, and daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, were reportedly traveling to a family baptism ceremony in California. Their lawyer, Olia Catala, stated they had no criminal record and were seeking asylum in the U.S., where they had lived since 2015. ICE claimed Mendoza overstayed his visa and that Mejia hurled hot coffee at officers, potentially leading to charges of assaulting a federal officer. Alaska Airlines noted the operation occurred during a busy travel weekend without prior notice.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both report that Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred, and that it was dropped during the commotion. FOX News and Newsweek describe the incident as involving an alleged assault by Mejia, with FOX News citing DHS claims that she threw hot coffee at officers. The Guardian and CBS News attribute the characterization of the coffee incident to the attorney, Olia Catala, while FOX News and Newsweek attribute it to DHS. The Guardian and CBS News also note that Mejia had married a U.S. citizen and was in the process of adjusting her status, a detail not included in the FOX News account. The BBC and CBS News mention that the Port of Seattle was “outraged” by the incident, while FOX News and Newsweek do not include this detail.

Sources The Guardian · BBC · FOX News · CBS News · Newsweek

Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) report that Israeli military actions have caused widespread environmental contamination across Gaza, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos, and sewage posing long-term health risks. Hakeem Jeffries named House Speaker after Democrats secure historic majority

Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat, was nominated as the next House Speaker by House Democrats, securing his position with a large majority. Jeffries, who previously worked as a corporate litigator, has emphasized his faith and community ties, particularly in Brooklyn. His leadership style is described as collaborative, focusing on listening to members before formulating strategy. Democrats have gained a significant majority in the House, with 258 seats, the largest since 1992, following a sweeping midterm victory. The party plans to use its majority to push for legislative action on issues like healthcare, affordability, and immigration, while also launching investigations into the Trump administration.

Where the accounts differ

NPR describes Jeffries as a strategic, deliberate politician with a focus on listening and avoiding ideological pigeonholing. The Hill highlights the challenges Jeffries faces with a large and diverse caucus, including balancing the interests of moderate and progressive members. CBS News and FOX News both note the historic nature of the Democratic majority, with CBS emphasizing the 258-seat tally and FOX mentioning the defeat of Virginia Foxx. The Daily Wire focuses on the diminished influence of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) due to the large Democratic majority, noting only eight DSA-affiliated members in the House. The New York Post and The Hill both mention the DSA's potential impact on policy, but The New York Post does not reference the DSA's influence, while The Hill does.

Sources NPR · The Hill · New York Post · CBS News · FOX News · The Daily Wire

Russian warship sinks off Libya as suspected Ukrainian strikes take war beyond Black Sea

Ukraine claims to have launched a drone attack on a Russian warship docked at a naval base in Benghazi, Libya, resulting in the vessel's sinking. President Zelenskyy stated that seven Ukrainian naval drones were used in the operation, which also targeted a Russian cargo ship. Libyan officials confirmed an explosion at the naval base, with satellite images showing the warship capsizing and sinking. The vessel, the Merkury, was reportedly refueling and resupplying under a cooperation agreement with Libya's eastern-based government. Libyan authorities called for an international investigation into the attacks, emphasizing that Libya is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war.

The attack on the Russian warship and a commercial ship off the coast of Benghazi is part of a broader pattern of Ukrainian long-range strikes against Russian assets. Zelenskyy described the operation as "exemplary," highlighting Ukraine's ability to conduct such attacks from distant locations. The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the drone attacks, calling for an "immediate, independent and transparent investigation." Libyan officials also condemned the use of their territory for foreign conflicts, stating that Libya will not allow its ports or waters to be used as an arena for settling scores.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that a second drone attack hit a commercial ship off the coast of Benghazi, with Libyan military officials attributing the attack to Ukrainian sea drones launched from a base in western Libya. NPR and Al Jazeera also mention the attack on the commercial ship, but Al Jazeera notes that the Libyan health ministry confirmed all crew members were rescued and in stable condition. CBS News and BBC do not specify the number of injured on the commercial ship, while The Guardian mentions that the number of injured and their nationalities are not known. Additionally, FOX News and The Guardian attribute the attack on the warship to Ukrainian drones, while BBC and CBS News do not explicitly state who launched the drones, though they cite Zelenskyy's claims.

Sources FOX News · NPR · Al Jazeera · CBS News · BBC · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Wash. officials condemn ICE after 2 arrested boarding flight at Seattle airport

Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers detained two individuals while they were boarding an Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday. The incident, captured on video by onlookers, showed plainclothes officers in masks detaining the individuals on the jet bridge. A woman was heard saying she and the other person had work permits. The Port of Seattle stated the incident occurred as travelers boarded a flight to Los Angeles. The Department of Homeland Security claimed the arrest was part of a targeted operation against Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who overstayed his visa. During the arrest, another passenger allegedly hurled hot coffee at the officers, leading to charges of assaulting a federal officer. The attorney representing the detained individuals, Olia Catala, stated they entered the country legally and have no criminal records. Washington Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson and Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson condemned the incident, calling the tactics used "unacceptable and un-American."

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and CBS News both report that the two individuals detained were a father and daughter, while The Guardian and BBC do not explicitly state this relationship, though they mention the individuals as a family. The Guardian and BBC note that the father and daughter were traveling to a family baptism ceremony and seeking asylum, a detail not included in ABC News or CBS News. The Guardian and BBC also mention that Mejia had married a U.S. citizen and was in the process of adjusting her status, which is not stated in ABC News or CBS News. FOX News and the New York Post do not mention the family relationship or the baptism ceremony. The Guardian and BBC also include quotes from Olia Catala about the coffee being spilled due to panic, which is not mentioned in ABC News or CBS News.

Sources ABC News · CBS News · The Guardian · BBC · FOX News · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump, Putin, and Xi met in Shenzhen for a trilateral summit

President Donald Trump met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference. The summit, described by some as historic, included a roundtable discussion among the three leaders. The meeting resulted in a four-point declaration focusing on peace, strategic stability, and further dialogue, though it lacked specific commitments on nuclear arms limits, verification, or Ukraine and Iran. Trump referred to Putin as a “friend” during the meeting, a characterization that drew both domestic and international criticism. The U.S. intelligence chief, Jay Clayton, defended Trump’s remarks, calling them “entirely appropriate” for building a personal rapport with the Russian leader.

The summit also drew attention for its implications on U.S. foreign policy. Military analyst Phillips O'Brien noted that the U.S. appears to be moving closer to Russia than to Ukraine or its European allies, suggesting that Ukraine's support will increasingly rely on Europe. O'Brien criticized the U.S. for hampering Ukraine's defense capabilities through actions like shooting down drones, which he said undermines Ukraine's ability to defend itself.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both report that the summit produced no nuclear arms limits, no verification provisions, no negotiating timetable, and no agreement on Ukraine or Iran. The Daily Caller and The Dispatch, however, emphasize the lack of concrete commitments and the potential implications for U.S. foreign policy, with The Dispatch framing the meeting as a sign of America’s “slide into an amoral foreign policy.” The Al Jazeera and The Guardian accounts highlight the controversy over Trump’s characterization of Putin as a “friend,” with The Guardian noting that Clayton explicitly stated Putin is not America’s friend in Ukraine. The Daily Caller includes a quote from Senator John Kennedy describing Putin and Xi as “predators” who want to “eat America’s liver with some fava beans and a nice Chianti,” a characterization not present in other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · Al Jazeera · The Dispatch · NPR · The Guardian · The Daily Caller

US Army invokes emergency powers to detonate lead in Iowa

The US Army plans to detonate 68 barrels of lead azide, a toxic explosive, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. The operation is scheduled for Wednesday, November 25, 2026, to allow for optimal weather conditions and mitigation measures. The Army claims it must act under emergency powers to bypass a court order that temporarily halted the detonation. The court had issued a stay after environmental groups sued, arguing the Army failed to consider safer alternatives. The Army and its interagency partners say the detonation is necessary to prevent an uncontrolled explosion as temperatures are expected to drop below 30°F.

Environmental groups, including the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club, have criticized the Army’s decision, arguing that the court order was issued to ensure transparency and public safety. They claim the Army did not provide sufficient notice to affected communities and that the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is not as imminent as the Army claims. The Army has advised people to avoid the area during the detonation and urged those who cannot leave to take precautions.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and CBS News both state the detonation is scheduled for Wednesday, November 25, 2026, while the Washington Examiner and BBC report the Army planned to act by Tuesday, November 24. The Guardian and BBC mention the Army had initially planned the detonation for Friday, November 20, but later moved it to Monday, November 23, before the court intervened. The Washington Examiner and BBC note the Army had previously postponed the plan due to public outcry, while the New York Post and CBS News attribute the delay to the court order. The Guardian and BBC also mention the Army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored, making the explosives more vulnerable to temperature changes, a detail not included in the other accounts.

Sources New York Post · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · CBS News · BBC

Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels

International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed on Sunday after a dispute over whether to explicitly mention fossil fuels in the final agreement. Delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach a consensus, with the European Union and several other nations rejecting a draft that did not include explicit language on phasing out fossil fuels. The talks, which ran two days longer than expected, became the longest climate conference in the history of these summits. The EU, represented by Ireland's Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O'Brien, walked out of the room in protest, citing the need to address fossil fuels as the main cause of global warming. The final agreement failed to include a commitment to transition away from fossil fuels, which make up roughly 73% of global emissions.

The failure to reach an agreement highlights deep divisions between nations. Some oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed language that would require a transition away from fossil fuels. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.5 degrees Celsius warming would require cutting emissions by 45% by 2035, which would necessitate a dramatic reduction in fossil fuel use. Meanwhile, Australia's climate and energy minister Chris Bowen stated that the transition away from fossil fuels is happening regardless of what the U.N. agreements say.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and CBS News both report that the EU, represented by Ireland's Darragh O'Brien, rejected the draft agreement for not mentioning fossil fuels. Fox Business adds that the draft omitted fossil fuels entirely and instead focused on carbon capture and climate finance, which was also a point of contention. BBC notes that while the central agreement failed, some other items on the agenda were agreed upon, including a just transition framework and a pledge to increase electricity's share of global energy use to 35% by 2035. Axios highlights the broader implications of the failure, including calls for reforming the COP process and the role of fossil fuels in climate change.

Sources NPR · CBS News · Fox Business · BBC · Axios

No source labeled left or right covered this story.

Trump orders contractors to check with White House over any congressional inquiries

President Donald Trump issued an executive order directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with the White House before responding to congressional inquiries. The order mandates that companies withhold communications deemed privileged by the administration and coordinate with the White House on "appropriate responses" to such requests. Non-compliance could result in contract termination or suspension of future federal work. The directive is part of the administration's strategy to resist anticipated aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats following their expected control of Congress in January. The White House has also instructed federal agencies to seek approval from its counsel before agreeing to congressional appearances.

White House Counsel Will Scharf informed agencies that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality," and he dismissed requests from Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, to preserve documents, arguing that Democrats are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and NPR both report that the executive order requires contractors to consult the White House and withhold privileged communications. The Washington Examiner and FOX News also describe similar directives, though the Examiner's account is more limited in detail. The Guardian and NPR mention that the order is part of the administration's effort to resist Democratic oversight, while FOX News adds that the order is framed as pushback against lawmakers "harassing private companies" to obtain confidential information. The Guardian and NPR attribute the claim about "blatant criminality" to Scharf, while FOX News attributes it to the White House in general. The Examiner does not mention Scharf's comments or the "blatant criminality" characterization.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · Washington Examiner · FOX News

Denmark to expel Russian diplomat over alleged plot to kill US-Ukrainian rapper

Denmark’s foreign minister, Lars Løkke Rasmussen, announced the expulsion of Russia’s defense attache in Copenhagen following allegations that Moscow was behind an attempted assassination of a US-Ukrainian rapper, Kyivstoner, in September. Danish police thwarted the plot by arresting three men linked to the Danish criminal underworld shortly before Kyivstoner was set to perform at a concert. A fourth suspect was arrested later that evening. The suspects are charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service. Rasmussen also mentioned Denmark’s consideration of suspending Schengen visas for Russians and urged the EU to adopt a unified approach to visa restrictions. The Russian embassy in Copenhagen denied the accusations, stating they lack proof.

According to Danish security services, the suspects were driving toward the concert venue with weapons when they were intercepted by police. One of the suspects had purchased a ticket to the event. Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, head of Denmark’s national security and intelligence service, confirmed that the assassination attempt was planned by Russian intelligence services. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen expressed solidarity with Denmark and called for a new European security strategy to enhance preparedness and deterrence.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that Denmark’s foreign minister sent a message to senior European diplomats proposing the EU halt tourist visas for Russians and cease recognition of Russian non-biometric passports. FOX News states that the two suspects charged pleaded guilty, while The Guardian notes they denied wrongdoing. FOX News also mentions that Russia accused Kyivstoner of planning a drone attack on Moscow, an allegation The Guardian does not include. The Guardian attributes the claim about Russia’s FSB accusing Kyivstoner to Russian media outlet Meduza, which FOX News does not cite. The Guardian and FOX News both mention the Russian embassy denying the accusations, but FOX News adds that Russia called the accusations "unsubstantiated."

Sources The Guardian · FOX News · NPR

Environmental crimes: Israel blamed for toxic pollution in 99% of Gaza

A report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) claims Israel’s military actions in Gaza have contaminated air, water, soil and food across more than 99% of the territory. The report, which uses satellite imagery and scientific analysis, highlights the long-term health risks to Palestinians, including exposure to toxins through multiple pathways. The report also notes the urgent need for an independent investigation into the environmental damage. The report comes amid ongoing international legal proceedings, including a case at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) regarding genocide.

The report details the environmental impact of Israel’s bombardment, including the release of pollutants from explosions, fires and rubble. It estimates that the Israeli military operations have generated over 61 million tonnes of debris, with 29 tonnes of rubble per person in Gaza. The report also mentions the destruction of sanitation systems, leading to raw sewage leaking into the environment and posing further health risks.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that Israel’s military actions have led to the destruction of over 80% of Gaza’s homes, with 350,000 families homeless. Anthropic's $1.5 trillion IPO sets off a fresh wave of tech wealth heading for South Florida

Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, went public on Thursday with an IPO priced at $83 per share, marking one of the largest public listings in history. The stock initially surged before sliding amid broader market declines. The IPO has sparked discussions about the potential migration of tech professionals and investors to South Florida, where real estate insiders predict a significant influx of wealth. Developers and executives like BH Group CEO Isaac Toledano and West Palm Beach developer Kenneth Baboun suggest that newly liquid tech workers and institutional backers are considering relocating to Florida due to high taxes in states like California and New York. The IPO is also expected to generate substantial wealth for Anthropic employees, with approximately 96% of the workforce becoming millionaires.

The IPO has drawn attention for its massive scale and the implications for wealth distribution. Mother Jones reports that over 5,100 Anthropic employees are now millionaires, with some analysts suggesting the wealth could strain San Francisco's housing market. The article also highlights the broader economic impact, noting that the wealth concentration in the hands of Anthropic insiders may exacerbate existing inequalities, as the poorest half of Americans hold less wealth than the company's employees.

Where the accounts differ

Fox Business reports that Kenneth Baboun and Isaac Toledano predict a tech exodus to South Florida by mid-to-end of 2027, citing high taxes in California and New York and the "point of no return" for those seeking to avoid government overreach. Mother Jones, however, omits any mention of Florida or migration, instead focusing on the wealth transfer to Anthropic employees and its impact on American poverty. Fox Business also includes quotes from Baboun and Toledano, while Mother Jones attributes its claims about wealth concentration to unnamed sources and does not include direct quotes from individuals.

Sources Fox Business · Mother Jones · Slate · Washington Examiner · The Daily Caller · The Nation

Trump says FBI hack might expose Russia "hoax"

President Trump on Saturday said the reported hack of a crucial FBI database might have a silver lining — it could, he claimed, expose more details of what he called the "Russia Russia Russia hoax." Trump made the comments during a Fox News interview, where he acknowledged the breach as "not good" but suggested it could reveal information about past investigations. The FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a database used by law enforcement agencies nationwide, was reportedly hacked, according to CNN and ABC News. The breach follows other cyber incidents affecting the FAA, NSA, and USDA in recent weeks.

The NCIC is a repository of criminal justice information, including data on criminal records, fugitives, stolen property, and missing persons. Law enforcement sources confirmed the hack to ABC News, though the FBI has not publicly commented. Trump suggested the breach might provide insight into investigations related to Russian interference in the 2016 election and the Ukraine phone call, which he has repeatedly labeled a "hoax." He also mentioned voter fraud, though the NCIC does not contain information about those specific investigations.

Where the accounts differ

Axios and The Daily Wire both report Trump suggested the hack might reveal information about the "Russia Russia Russia hoax" and the "Ukraine hoax," while ABC News and The Hill note Trump implied the hack could uncover details about the Russia-related investigations and the Ukraine phone call. The Daily Wire and The Hill mention Trump's comments about the USDA cyber incident and the firing of Sean Cairncross, which are not included in Axios or ABC News. The New York Post reports the NCIC was targeted for the second time in months and mentions the ShinyHunters group, which is not covered in other accounts.

Sources Axios · ABC News · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · The Hill · New York Post

Mexico captures cartel leader listed as one of top 10 most wanted in US

Mexican authorities arrested Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” during a special forces raid in Sinaloa on Friday night. The operation involved a firefight with cartel gunmen, resulting in casualties. Meza Flores, who was on the FBI’s top 10 most wanted list, was transported to Mexico City after the arrest. Mexican officials stated that U.S. intelligence aided in the operation. The arrest is described as a significant blow to a major drug trafficking network.

The FBI has listed Meza Flores as one of its Ten Most Wanted fugitives, accusing him of drug trafficking and drug-related crimes. He was originally indicted in 2012 and faced multiple charges, including drug-trafficking violations and firearm possession. The U.S. Treasury placed sanctions on him in 2013, freezing his assets. The operation led to widespread panic in Guasave, with civilians fleeing gunfire and businesses being damaged.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and FOX News both mention that U.S. intelligence aided in the arrest, while The Guardian and NPR provide more detail on the casualties, including four Mexican soldiers killed. The Guardian and Al Jazeera report that 11 people were killed in total, including seven cartel gunmen and four soldiers, while NPR and FOX News mention seven cartel gunmen and four soldiers killed. The Daily Wire and The Guardian attribute the claim about the operation being conducted by elite military forces to Mexican authorities, while FOX News and The Guardian also note that the operation was carried out using stealth and surprise. The Daily Wire and The Guardian mention that Meza Flores was arrested alongside his top lieutenant, Germán Rolando Gálvez Meza, and José N, an alleged financial operator, while the Washington Examiner and FOX News also include these details. The Daily Wire and The Guardian provide more context about the Beltrán Leyva faction and its alliance with the Mayos, which the Washington Examiner and FOX News do not mention.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · NPR · FOX News · Al Jazeera

Grand Theft Auto VI appears to mock NFL sexual misconduct scandals in radio parody

Grand Theft Auto VI includes a satirical segment featuring a fictional conservative talk radio station that mirrors real-life NFL sexual misconduct allegations. The segment, voiced by comedian Stavros Halkias, portrays a sports talk host defending a fictional player accused of inappropriate behavior during a massage. The character argues that the player's natural physiological response is not his fault, blaming the therapist instead. The game's fictional scenario closely resembles allegations against Cleveland Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson and Kansas City Chiefs kicker Justin Tucker. The segment is part of Rockstar Games' broader depiction of a corrupt, hyper-masculine society. Deshaun Watson, a real-life NFL player, referenced GTA VI just a day before its release, noting that his teammates were preoccupied with the game.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Axios both mention the satirical radio segment and its resemblance to NFL sexual misconduct allegations. The Guardian specifically notes that neither Watson nor Tucker are named in the game, while Axios does not mention the segment at all. Slate and Fox Business focus on the game's release and commercial success, omitting the satirical content. The Free Press does not mention the game's content or the NFL allegations. BBC highlights the game's potential real-world consequences and police warnings, but does not reference the satirical segment.

Sources The Guardian · Slate · Axios · BBC · The Free Press · Fox Business

White House replaces national cyber director amid widespread tech outages

The White House has replaced National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross with Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies. The move comes after a week of technology outages affecting major companies and government agencies. The Trump administration has stated that the outages are not the result of a cyberattack or state-sponsored activity, but rather due to system upgrades and patches.

The National Security Agency’s highly classified internal communications network, known as NSA Net, experienced a nearly four-day outage. Employees at the agency’s headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland, were unable to log in for most of the week, with some returning to work at staggered times to prevent overwhelming the system. The agency attributed the disruption to routine maintenance and software updates, though the process took longer than expected.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and The Hill both report that Sean Cairncross was replaced by Kirsten Davies, with ABC citing a source that President Trump believed Cairncross lacked strong cyber credentials. The Hill adds that Cairncross reportedly clashed with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over AI concerns and that Sen. Thom Tillis blocked a CISA nominee. The Daily Wire and FOX News mention the NSA outage but do not name the new cyber director. Mother Jones does not mention the NSA outage or the director replacement, focusing instead on criticism of the Trump administration. The New York Post details the NSA outage and links it to software patches for PHP vulnerabilities, which is not mentioned in other accounts.

Sources ABC News · The Hill · The Daily Wire · Mother Jones · FOX News · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump on credit card interest rate cap: ‘I would do it’

President Donald Trump stated during an interview with Fox News’ Kayleigh McEnany on "Saturday in America" that he would support a one-year cap on credit card interest rates at 10%. The proposal, previously mentioned by Trump in January, aligns with support from both Democrats and Republicans, including Sen. Josh Hawley and Sen. Elizabeth Warren. Trump argued that credit card companies charge excessive fees and interest, which he claims rip off consumers.

The proposal to cap credit card interest rates at 10% would significantly reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve. With rates at 10%, a cardholder with a $5,000 balance would pay about $42 per month in interest, compared to $100 per month at the current average rate. Trump’s comments come as credit card balances have surged to a record $1.29 trillion, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Daily Caller both report that Trump said he would support a one-year cap at 10%, while The Hill and Axios mention the same but include additional context about the average interest rate and the Federal Reserve’s data. The CBS News account provides more detail on the financial impact, including the $100 billion annual savings estimate and the $160 billion in interest charges. The Axios account also notes that the banking industry opposes the cap, arguing it would limit credit access. The Daily Caller includes a quote from Elizabeth Warren on X, which is not present in the other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · Fox Business · CBS News · Axios · The Hill · The Daily Caller

No source labeled left covered this story.

Second judge to block Trump's contested D.C. arch

A second federal judge has issued a preliminary injunction blocking construction on President Trump's proposed 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery. U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema of Virginia called the project a "rushed job" lacking a legal basis. The injunction will indefinitely halt the project while the court considers the lawsuit. This follows a separate order from D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, who extended her temporary restraining order blocking construction until December 3. Both judges have cited concerns over the project's legal authority, environmental impact, and potential disruption to traffic and historical sightlines.

The National Park Service has supported the project, stating it would not alter historic views, while the FAA deemed the arch safe for air travel. However, the National Capital Planning Commission, which approved the project, has faced criticism for its composition of Trump loyalists. The White House has defended the arch as a tribute to veterans and a fitting monument, with a spokesperson stating the administration is confident it will be vindicated in court. The Justice Department has announced plans to appeal Brinkema's decision.

Where the accounts differ

Axios and Newsweek both report that Judge Brinkema called the project a "rushed job" and that the National Park Service did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. The Guardian and NPR note that Brinkema criticized the administration's argument about congressional approval from 1925, while the New York Post adds that Trump claimed the arch would serve as a "top grade Military Complex" with drone and sniper capabilities. Newsweek and The Guardian mention the Kennedy family's lawsuit, while the New York Post provides more detail on the arch's design and Trump's claims about its military function. Axios and NPR state that the National Park Service defended the federal review process, while the Guardian and Newsweek highlight concerns about the arch's impact on historic sightlines.

Sources Axios · Newsweek · The Guardian · NPR · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Top House Democrat questions what Trump accomplished in Xi-Putin summit

Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, criticized President Trump's recent summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling it a missed opportunity for meaningful diplomacy. Meeks argued that the meeting failed to produce agreements on critical issues like nuclear arms control and artificial intelligence safety, and warned that the discussions could undermine U.S. alliances. He also expressed concern that the summit may have encouraged the leaders to divide the world into spheres of influence. Meeks called for U.S. diplomats to have raised concerns about Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft before the summit to set clear goals for the talks. He also urged reducing tariffs on U.S. allies while pressuring China to end its support for Russia's war in Ukraine.

Trump, in a White House press conference, defended the summit, calling it a historic diplomatic milestone. He emphasized the importance of dialogue among rival nuclear powers and claimed the meeting offered an opportunity to address long-standing issues. However, he did not provide specific details on what was discussed or any agreements reached. The summit took place during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting, where Trump also highlighted his achievements in trade and diplomacy.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that Meeks questioned the lack of meaningful agreements on nuclear weapons and AI safety, and that he called for reducing tariffs on U.S. allies. The Hill notes that Trump's press conference included a defensive tone over the midterms and a controversial remark about Putin being his "friend." FOX News states that Trump described the summit as a diplomatic milestone and emphasized the importance of dialogue among nuclear powers. CBS News focuses on Trump's praise for his chief of staff Stephen Miller and his threats to veto Democratic legislation. The Christian Science Monitor highlights that Putin benefited most from the summit, with Trump publicly calling him "my friend." The New York Post mentions that the summit produced a joint declaration on nuclear risks and energy supplies but stopped short of major breakthroughs on Ukraine or Iran.

Sources NPR · The Hill · FOX News · CBS News · Christian Science Monitor · New York Post

Man accused of sparking deadly Los Angeles wildfire found guilty

A 30-year-old man, Jonathan Rinderknecht, was found guilty of two federal arson charges in a retrial for the 2025 Palisades Fire, which killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes. Prosecutors argued that Rinderknecht, a former Uber driver, intentionally started a brush fire in the Santa Monica Mountains near Pacific Palisades on January 1, 2025. The fire, initially called the Lachman Fire, smoldered underground and reignited as the Palisades Fire on January 7, 2025, fueled by strong winds. The fire burned over 23,000 acres and caused extensive damage. Rinderknecht was arrested in Florida nine months after the fire. During the retrial, jurors were instructed not to consider the adequacy of the fire department’s response to the Lachman and Palisades blaze. The defense argued that the fire was ignited by fireworks, but prosecutors dismissed this as "baseless." The conviction follows a mistrial in the first trial, where jurors were deadlocked.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Hill both report that Rinderknecht called 911 multiple times after the Lachman Fire began, while CBS News and ABC News also mention this detail. The Guardian and The Hill state that Rinderknecht was at the bottom of a hiking trail when he saw the Lachman Fire, but ABC News and FOX News note that geolocation data showed he was 30 feet away from the flames. The Guardian and The Hill describe Rinderknecht as a disgruntled young man seeking retribution for personal grievances, while BBC and ABC News attribute this characterization to prosecutors. The Guardian and The Hill mention that the defense argued the fire was ignited by fireworks, but CBS News and ABC News do not include this claim. The Guardian and The Hill report that the fire department failed to fully extinguish the Lachman Fire, while FOX News and ABC News do not mention this. The Guardian and The Hill state that the fire was fully contained on January 31, 2025, while CBS News and ABC News report the same date. The Guardian and The Hill mention that the fire destroyed 6,800 structures, while CBS News and ABC News report 16,000 structures destroyed. The Guardian and The Hill report that the fire was the third most destructive in state history, while CBS News and ABC News do not mention this. The Guardian and The Hill report that the fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region, while BBC and ABC News do not mention this.

Sources The Guardian · CBS News · BBC · The Hill · FOX News · ABC News

Zohran Mamdani unveils plan to close Rikers Island jail complex

Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced a plan to close the Rikers Island jail complex by the end of 2032, with the goal of relocating its remaining jail population. The plan includes building four new borough-based jails in Brooklyn, the Bronx, Queens, and Manhattan, with the Brooklyn facility opening in 2029 and the Manhattan facility by 2032. The city aims to reduce the jail population from around 6,600 to no more than 4,100 by 2032. The plan also includes investments in mental health care, substance use treatment, and therapeutic housing for individuals with serious medical needs. The city faces a legally mandated deadline to close Rikers by August 2027, but Mamdani’s administration states it will require new legislation to extend the deadline.

The plan has faced criticism from some correction officers’ unions, which argue that reducing the jail population to 4,100 could jeopardize public safety. The city has also acknowledged delays in construction and an increase in jail population since 2020, which has raised concerns about meeting the capacity of the new facilities. The federal government previously placed Rikers under the control of an independent remediation manager, and Mamdani’s plan includes working with that official to bring the closure to fruition.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Daily Wire both mention the 2019 legislation requiring Rikers to close by 2027, while The Daily Caller and FOX News refer to the same legislation but state that the original deadline was August 2027. The Guardian and The Daily Wire note that the city is not on track to meet the 2027 deadline, while The Daily Caller and FOX News state that the original deadline was August 2027 and that Mamdani’s plan delays it to 2032. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller mention the estimated cost of the project rising from $8.7 billion to $16 billion, while The Guardian and BBC do not mention the cost increase. The Guardian and BBC report that the four new facilities are expected to have about 4,500 beds, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller state that the new facilities are designed to accommodate around 4,500 inmates.

Sources The Guardian · NPR · BBC · FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Senate Republicans reject war powers resolution to end Iran conflict

Senate Republicans on Thursday blocked a measure that would have directed President Trump to end hostilities in Iran. The vote failed 48-51. GOP Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Rand Paul (Ky.), who have voted for previous resolutions directing Trump to end the war, joined almost the entire Democratic caucus. Centrist Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), an ardent supporter of Israel, was the only Democrat to vote against it. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who voted for the resolution in September, voted against the current version. The measure, known as a war powers resolution, is mostly a signaling vote. Democrats wanted to put Republicans on the record voting against ending the war, even though if the resolution had passed, Trump likely would not have signed it. Thursday’s vote was the first time either chamber voted on the war powers resolution since the November midterms. The House passed a complementary resolution in mid-September, led by Rep. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.), by a vote of 220-204. Seven Republicans joined Democrats in that case to limit Trump’s military actions against Iran.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill reports that the war powers resolution failed 48-51, while FOX News does not mention the vote outcome. CBS News and Axios focus on the potential for a government shutdown in December if funding for the Iran war is not restricted. The Hill and CBS News both mention the cost of the war, with The Hill citing $48.3 billion as of Nov. 13, while CBS News does not include a specific figure. FOX News focuses on internal Democratic Party conflicts and far-left activism, which the other accounts do not mention. The Hill and Axios both mention Reps. Yassamin Ansari and Ro Khanna opposing funding packages that do not prohibit funds from being used for offensive operations in Iran, while FOX News does not mention these specific lawmakers or their positions.

Sources The Hill · FOX News · CBS News · Axios · Washington Examiner · NPR

No source labeled left covered this story.

Judge approves $7.25bn Bayer payout to settle claims that Roundup causes cancer

A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits alleging that its weedkiller Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has weighed on the German company for close to a decade. Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate.” The settlement will be paid to Roundup users who are already sick with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who fall ill in the future. The settlement excludes some lawsuits that remain pending in federal court. Bayer has faced approximately 65,000 claims in US state and federal courts from people who said they developed cancer after using Roundup at home or on the job.

The settlement was approved five months after the US Supreme Court overturned a $1.25m jury award for a Missouri man, John Durnell, who blamed years of exposure to glyphosate in Roundup for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The court ruled 7-2, saying Bayer cannot be sued in state courts because federal regulations do not mandate a cancer warning label. The settlement comes after the Supreme Court in June ruled in favour of Bayer, overturning a $1.25m settlement for a Missouri man who said Roundup and its ingredient glyphosate was to blame for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and BBC both state the settlement is $7.25bn, while the Washington Examiner and Just The News refer to it as $7 billion. The New York Post also mentions $7.25bn but attributes the figure to the settlement amount. The Guardian and BBC mention that the settlement excludes some lawsuits that remain pending in federal court, while the New York Post states that about 200,000 Roundup-related claims have been made against Bayer, many coming from people who used it on residential lawns and gardens. The Guardian and BBC note that the settlement includes $600 million for attorneys’ fees, which the Washington Examiner and Just The News omit. The New York Post and BBC mention that the International Agency for Research on Cancer classified glyphosate as “probably carcinogenic” in 2015, while the Guardian and Washington Examiner do not include this detail.

Sources The Guardian · Washington Examiner · BBC · Just The News · New York Post

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

The U.K. and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties

The U.K. and EU held a summit in Brussels to discuss closer cooperation and trade agreements. Prime Minister Andy Burnham met with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The summit aimed to address issues such as youth mobility, food trade, and emissions standards. Burnham emphasized the benefits of a closer partnership with Europe, including lower food prices and economic growth. The agreements reached are expected to add 0.4% to Britain's economy. The summit also included discussions on security and defense cooperation, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that the summit includes an agreement for up to 100,000 young adults from Britain to live and work in EU countries and the same number of Europeans to come to the U.K. The Guardian mentions a compromise on tuition fees for EU students, with the EU dropping its demand for home fees and agreeing to a supplementary agreement for further negotiations. BBC states that the UK and EU will allow up to 100,000 young people from each side to live and work in the other’s countries. Al Jazeera mentions the same number but adds that the details of student fees remain a work in progress. The Guardian also reports that the UK and EU plan to establish formal talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries, which is not mentioned in the other accounts.

Sources NPR · The Guardian · BBC · Al Jazeera · Christian Science Monitor

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Democrats secure majority in House, Republicans face internal calls for accountability

Democrats achieved a significant victory in the 2026 midterm elections, with 56% of voters supporting them in House races compared to 42% for Republicans, according to NPR. This marks the largest win for either party in 50 years, surpassing previous margins from 2006 and 2018. The Democratic gains resulted in flipping 46 House seats, potentially reaching 49, and could lead to the largest House majority since the early 1990s.

In response to the election results, House Speaker Mike Johnson urged Republicans to remain engaged and attend sessions to advance their legislative agenda before Democrats take control. Johnson highlighted the need for full attendance to pass key priorities, including government funding and the National Defense Authorization Act. Some Republican members, including Rep. Thomas Massie, criticized their colleagues for skipping work while still receiving pay, noting that the House had to adjourn early due to insufficient attendance.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that Democrats secured a 14-point margin in House races, while The Daily Caller and Axios mention that 14 Republican members missed votes, leading to adjournments. FOX News and The Daily Caller note that Massie criticized Republicans for skipping work and still collecting pay, a detail not included in NPR or Newsweek. Newsweek includes quotes from political scientist Grant Reeher, which are absent from other accounts. Axios and The Daily Caller specify that 11 of the 14 absent Republicans will not return in January, a detail not mentioned in NPR or FOX News.

Sources NPR · Newsweek · FOX News · The Daily Caller · Axios

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Russia's retaliatory barrage on Kyiv bridges threatens civilian safety and disrupts Ukraine's infrastructure, escalating regional conflict with far-reaching consequences.

Russia attacks Kyiv bridges and infrastructure in major strike

Russia launched a major missile and drone attack on Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine, targeting bridges, energy facilities, and railway stations. Ukrainian officials reported at least nine deaths and 28 injuries, with Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko noting damage to three main bridges over the Dnipro River. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as "one of the largest" of the war, with Russia firing over 110 missiles and more than 400 drones. Russia’s Defence Ministry claimed it targeted bridges used for military logistics and energy infrastructure. Poland reported three objects, likely two missiles and a drone, entered its airspace during the attack.

The attack followed Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Crimean Bridge, which Russia has called a "prized" symbol of its annexation of Crimea. Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed a "far more painful" response to the bridge attack, which Ukraine claimed damaged the road section. Zelenskyy said the strike on the bridge was part of a weeks-long operation to weaken its defenses. Russia’s Defence Ministry also reported intercepting 310 Ukrainian drones during the attack.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and BBC both report that Russia targeted Kyiv’s bridges and infrastructure, with Al Jazeera citing eight deaths and 28 injuries, while BBC states at least nine deaths and unspecified injuries. FOX News reports that Putin vowed a "far more painful" response to the Crimean Bridge attack, a claim not made by Al Jazeera or BBC. The Guardian, however, focuses on Kyiv residents’ reactions to the bridge damage, noting that the Northern Bridge remained open for public transport. BBC also mentions that Russia’s strikes coincided with talks around the war, while Al Jazeera and FOX News include details about the U.S. involvement and negotiations.

Sources Al Jazeera · FOX News · BBC · The Guardian
