Elon Musk claims ‘I’m not Maga’ and says he regrets vast sums to back Republicans

Elon Musk denied being associated with the "Make America Great Again" (MAGA) movement during a virtual appearance at the New York Times Dealbook Summit. He admitted to spending nearly $500 million on Republican candidates in the 2026 midterms, which he called a "failed" effort. Musk also expressed regret over his financial support for Trump's re-election campaign in 2024, which cost him at least $250 million. He stated that he felt "pretty foolish" about the amount spent, arguing that campaign cash alone cannot determine election outcomes. Musk also distanced himself from the Republican Party's base, saying he does not share "blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party."

Musk, who previously described himself as "dark, gothic MAGA" at a 2024 Trump rally, now claims he is "not MAGA." He also criticized Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for allegedly lying about restrictions on his Starshield satellite system. Musk further stated that his interactions with Anthropic were positive, calling the AI firm "good people" and "principled." He also mentioned that he had served for 180 days as head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) under Trump’s administration before leaving due to a public falling-out.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Al Jazeera both report Musk said he felt "pretty foolish" about his spending, but The Guardian adds that Musk admitted his spending had "failed" and that he felt "pretty foolish" for spending so much. The Hill and BBC also mention Musk feeling "foolish," but The Hill provides a specific figure of $442 million, while The Guardian and Al Jazeera cite $500 million and $446 million respectively. The Guardian and The Hill both mention Musk’s previous identification with MAGA, but The Guardian includes the specific quote from the 2024 rally, while The Hill adds context about the black MAGA hat and its association with Nazi symbolism. The Washington Examiner does not mention Musk’s comments on MAGA or his spending, focusing instead on the DOJ’s action in the Alaska Senate race.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera · CBS News · BBC · The Hill · Washington Examiner

Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share ahead of stock market debut

Anthropic, an artificial intelligence company, priced its initial public offering at $83 per share on Wednesday. The company is expected to start trading on the Nasdaq Composite under the ticker symbol ANT on Thursday. The IPO is anticipated to value Anthropic at approximately $1.5 trillion, making it one of the most significant stock market debuts in history. The offering includes the sale of $65 billion in shares to the public and an additional $26 billion to institutional investors.

The IPO has sparked significant market reactions, with Asian stock markets experiencing sharp declines as concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom persist. Investors are questioning whether the high valuations of AI companies are justified, given the potential for a market correction similar to past tech bubbles.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and BBC both report that Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share and is expected to trade on the Nasdaq Composite. However, the BBC adds that the IPO is aimed at a valuation of $1.4 trillion, while the Washington Examiner states $1.5 trillion. The BBC also notes that the IPO is the largest money-raising event in US corporate history, a claim not made by the Washington Examiner. The Al Jazeera article reports that Asian stock markets fell sharply in response to the IPO, while the Washington Examiner does not mention market reactions. The BBC and Al Jazeera also highlight concerns about the AI bubble, which are absent in the Washington Examiner's account.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Dispatch · The Free Press · BBC · Al Jazeera · Mother Jones

Trump’s Pick to Run America’s Cyber Defense Agency Doesn’t Think January 6 Was an Attack

Michael LoSapio, nominated for director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), testified during a Senate hearing that he does not believe the Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021. LoSapio, who works for Palantir, a defense tech company, was questioned by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D–Conn.) about the 2020 election. LoSapio refused to confirm that Joe Biden won the popular vote, leading Blumenthal to accuse him of lacking independence and objectivity. LoSapio’s nomination has raised concerns among cybersecurity professionals due to his lack of government experience and potential loyalty to Trump. The hearing occurred amid a series of tech outages, including FAA ground stops and banking disruptions, which have raised questions about the nation’s cybersecurity readiness.

The White House has fired Sean Cairncross, the former national cyber director, and appointed Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, as acting director. The White House cited concerns over Cairncross’s cyber credentials, though no specific reasons were given. Davies will oversee cybersecurity policy across the federal government. The firings come amid a wave of tech outages that have disrupted critical services, with officials attributing the incidents to technical issues rather than cyberattacks.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones reports that LoSapio refused to confirm Biden won the 2020 popular vote, while The Hill and Washington Examiner do not mention this specific claim. The Hill and Washington Examiner state that the White House fired Cairncross due to concerns over his credentials, but Mother Jones does not specify the reason. Fox Business and The Daily Wire describe a series of tech outages affecting multiple sectors, while Mother Jones and The Hill attribute these outages to software upgrades and overloaded systems rather than cyberattacks. The Daily Wire includes additional, more detailed claims about the scope of outages and includes unverified events like the CIA headquarters fire, which are not mentioned in other accounts.

Sources Mother Jones · The Hill · Washington Examiner · Fox Business · FOX News · The Daily Wire

Army delays detonation in Iowa that could send toxic dust into Illinois

The U.S. Army has postponed plans to detonate unstable explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, after public and environmental concerns. Originally scheduled for Friday, November 20, the detonation was delayed to Monday, November 23, to avoid a forecasted temperature drop that could destabilize the material. The operation involves 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive used in military ammunition. The Army claims the material has deteriorated during storage, becoming increasingly sensitive to friction and shock. Environmental groups and local officials have raised concerns about the potential for toxic lead dust to spread across parts of Iowa and Illinois, affecting farmland, playgrounds, and residential areas. The Army has advised residents in the Middletown City Park neighborhood to temporarily leave the area during the detonation and recommends staying indoors with doors and windows closed to minimize exposure.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and The Guardian both report that the Army postponed the detonation to Monday, November 23, citing a forecasted temperature drop. The Daily Wire and BBC also mention the delay but do not specify the reason as clearly. The Daily Wire states the detonation was scheduled for Friday, November 20, while CBS News and The Guardian confirm the original date. The Guardian and BBC mention that the Army advised certain residents to evacuate between 8 a.m. and 2 p.m. CT, while CBS News and The Daily Wire provide more specific details about the evacuation window. The Daily Wire and The Guardian note that schools in the area have canceled classes, while CBS News and BBC mention this as well. The Daily Wire and The Guardian report that the Army has taken precautions like wetting surrounding soil to reduce dust, while CBS News and BBC mention air monitors and environmental sampling. The Daily Wire and The Guardian also note that the Army has recommended cleaning surfaces after the detonation, while CBS News and BBC mention similar advice.

Sources CBS News · The Daily Wire · Mother Jones · BBC · New York Post · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Beloved hippo Fiona dies days after swallowing hat

Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, died at the Cincinnati Zoo after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure. The zoo confirmed the death on Thursday, stating that despite efforts by veterinary and animal care teams, Fiona could not recover. The hat was tossed into the air by a visitor and caught on a ceiling fan, which launched it into Fiona’s habitat. The zoo attributed the incident to an accident. Fiona, who was born prematurely in 2017, had become a global sensation due to her survival and popularity. Her death has prompted widespread mourning from zoo staff, visitors, and public figures.

The Cincinnati Zoo's care team attempted various methods to help Fiona pass the hat, including using a vibration plate borrowed from a horse farm. Veterinarians also performed an ultrasound and a colonoscopy to assess Fiona's condition. Despite these efforts, Fiona's body could not fight the blockage, and she ultimately passed away. The zoo emphasized that surgery was not an option for a full-grown hippo due to the animal's size and thick skin.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and FOX News both report that Fiona's hat was tossed into the air by a visitor and caught on a ceiling fan, but FOX News includes a separate story about two bucks fighting in Redwood National Park, which CBS News does not. The Daily Wire mentions that a Tuesday ultrasound found “bunching of her intestines,” a detail not included in CBS News or FOX News. The Guardian and BBC both note that Fiona weighed around 2,500 pounds, while CBS News states she would have been 10 years old this January, and the Guardian adds that she weighed 2,500lb (1,113kg). The Guardian also mentions that Fiona was sedated a second time for evaluation, a detail not present in CBS News or FOX News.

Sources CBS News · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Newsweek · BBC · The Guardian

Myanmar becomes first state found responsible for genocide by UN court

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority during a 2017 military crackdown. The court found that the violence was intended to destroy the Rohingya population, resulting in thousands of deaths and the displacement of over 740,000 people to Bangladesh. The ruling, which was 9–6, marks the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide by the ICJ. The court ordered Myanmar to investigate and punish those responsible, provide reparations to the Rohingya, and allow refugees to return home. Myanmar has consistently denied allegations of mass rape, murder, and arson.

The court also acknowledged the ongoing conflict in Myanmar, which began with a 2021 military coup and has led to over 100,000 deaths and the displacement of 5.2 million people. The ruling could have significant implications for other genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel over alleged actions in Gaza.

Where the accounts differ

Axios and The Guardian both state that the ICJ ruled Myanmar committed genocide, while Al Jazeera and BBC describe the ruling as a verdict on whether Myanmar committed genocide. NPR and Christian Science Monitor also describe the ruling as a finding of genocide. Al Jazeera and BBC note that the case was brought by The Gambia on behalf of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, while Axios and The Guardian attribute the case to The Gambia directly. Al Jazeera and BBC mention the 2021 military coup and its impact, which Axios and The Guardian do not include. The Guardian and NPR provide specific numbers on the number of Rohingya killed and displaced, which are not included in Al Jazeera or BBC accounts. Axios and The Guardian attribute the ruling to the ICJ, while Al Jazeera and BBC describe it as a verdict.

Sources Axios · Al Jazeera · BBC · The Guardian · NPR · Christian Science Monitor

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Trump pardons late baseball great Pete Rose after historic China trip

President Donald Trump said Thursday he issued a "complete and total pardon" to baseball legend Pete Rose, who died in 2024. Trump posted the announcement to his social media platform as he was returning from his trip to Asia where he met with other world leaders, notably the first-ever trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia. Rose, who holds the Major League Baseball record for most career hits, was sentenced to five months in prison after being convicted of tax charges in 1990. He was also permanently banned from baseball in 1989 following an investigation into his betting on baseball games while managing the Cincinnati Reds. Rose was posthumously reinstated to MLB last year, making him eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame posthumously. Trump has previously said he wanted Rose to be pardoned and up for reconsideration for the Hall of Fame.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and The Guardian both state that Rose was banned from baseball in 1989, while CBS News and The Daily Wire mention the ban occurred in 1989 as well. The Guardian and The Daily Wire note that Rose was reinstated to MLB last year, while ABC News and CBS News state that Rose was reinstated last year. The Guardian and The Daily Wire mention that Rose was released from prison in 1991, while CBS News and The Daily Wire also note that Rose was released from prison in 1991. The Guardian and The Daily Wire state that Rose was posthumously reinstated to MLB last year, while ABC News and CBS News state that Rose was posthumously reinstated to MLB last year. The Guardian and The Daily Wire mention that Rose was released from prison in 1991, while CBS News and The Daily Wire also note that Rose was released from prison in 1991. The Guardian and The Daily Wire state that Rose was posthumously reinstated to MLB last year, while ABC News and CBS News state that Rose was posthumously reinstated to MLB last year.

Sources ABC News · BBC · The Daily Wire · CBS News · The Guardian · Just The News

Senate passes bipartisan permitting reform bill, sends legislation to the House

The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on a 62-33 vote, with 15 Democrats joining Republicans in supporting the legislation. The bill aims to streamline the permitting process for energy and infrastructure projects, including renewable energy, power lines, highways, and data centers. It also includes provisions to limit legal challenges and expedite project approvals. The legislation now moves to the House for further consideration. The White House has expressed support for the bill, and President Trump has endorsed it. Critics, including some Democrats and environmental groups, argue the bill weakens environmental protections and could lead to more fossil fuel projects.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that the bill could cut average residential power prices by 3%-4% in 2035, based on Rhodium Group estimates, and that Democratic co-authors and supporters emphasize easing clean energy buildout for future climate progress. Just The News states that Sheldon Whitehouse claimed the bill would save Americans approximately $60 to $80 each month. Christian Science Monitor notes that Whitehouse said the bill would have a more powerful climate effect in the power sector than the Inflation Reduction Act. FOX News and CBS News do not mention specific cost savings figures. Axios and CBS News both note that the bill includes provisions to ensure data centers pay for grid upgrades and have higher transmission service costs, while FOX News and Christian Science Monitor provide more detail on these provisions. The Christian Science Monitor and CBS News mention that the bill would change core aspects of environmental laws, including exemptions from NEPA review and the Clean Water Act, which are not detailed in Axios or FOX News.

Sources Axios · Washington Examiner · Just The News · Christian Science Monitor · FOX News · CBS News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Nvidia's halt of China AI chip shipments sparks national security concerns, disrupting global tech supply chains and escalating U.S.-China tech tensions.

Nvidia halts China AI chip shipments amid CEO scandal and national security concerns

Nvidia has stopped shipping certain advanced AI chips to China, according to reports. The company's interim CEO, Colette Kress, stated that it is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China. This decision comes after the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang, who stepped down amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The U.S. government had previously approved exports of certain Nvidia chips to China under specific conditions, but the company has now excluded Chinese data center sales from its revenue forecasts. The move has raised questions about the company's ability to serve the Chinese market despite changes to U.S. export rules.

The scandal has drawn attention to the broader implications of AI chip exports for national security. The Biden administration had imposed strict restrictions on the sale of advanced AI chips to China, but the Trump administration eased these restrictions, allowing for the export of certain Nvidia processors. This policy shift followed discussions between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and efforts by Huang to expand Nvidia's access to China. However, Beijing has also imposed its own restrictions on H200 imports, seeking to reduce its reliance on American semiconductor technology.

California has launched an investigation into whether Nvidia's exports of advanced chips ended up in China, violating U.S. restrictions. The state's attorney general, Rob Bonta, issued a subpoena to Nvidia, citing concerns about potential misleading investors and the transfer of confidential information to China. The investigation also looks into whether former CEO Huang's actions may have contributed to the unauthorized transfer of advanced chips or sensitive data.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that the Trump administration allowed the export of advanced AI chips to China, enabling a $60 billion transfer over 18 months, with some chips suspected of being smuggled into China. Fox Business states that Nvidia halted shipments to China despite U.S. approval, without clarifying the reason. The Daily Caller notes that Nvidia cut off shipments of Hopper chips to China after Huang's resignation, reversing efforts made by Huang to lobby the Trump administration. The Guardian highlights California's investigation into whether Nvidia's exports ended up in China, citing concerns about misleading investors and the transfer of confidential information.

Sources NPR · Fox Business · The Daily Caller · The Guardian

The brief ends here.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to Testify Before Congress on National Security Allegations

Jensen Huang, former CEO of Nvidia, is set to testify before Congress on December 1, according to a joint committee announcement. Huang will appear in closed-door sessions followed by Nvidia’s General Counsel Tim Teter, who will testify the next day. The committees involved include the Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the House Intelligence Committee. The chairmen of these committees stated they are seeking answers on Huang’s alleged role in a potential breach of national security, including his possible involvement with a Chinese intelligence asset.

Huang resigned from Nvidia after a second extramarital affair was revealed, following initial accusations of an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. Alice Huang is alleged to have been a spy for Beijing and facilitated the smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China. Huang agreed to cooperate with an internal investigation after his affair was first disclosed. The company announced it was searching for a new CEO and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. Nvidia also formed a national security and export control oversight committee on its board.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and The Guardian both report that Huang will testify on December 1, with Teter testifying the next day. The Guardian adds that Congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford, who chair the relevant committees, had previously warned Huang of potential subpoenas. The Guardian also details the involvement of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that allegedly facilitated $12bn in chip sales in violation of U.S. export controls. The Daily Wire mentions Trump’s praise for Nvidia’s new oversight committee but does not reference Megaspeed or the export control violations. The Guardian and The Daily Wire differ on the exact date of Huang’s resignation, with The Guardian stating it occurred on November 12 and The Daily Wire noting it was last Thursday, which would be November 10.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Guardian · NPR · Axios · Newsweek · BBC

Trump lands in China with key meetings with Xi and Putin on the agenda

President Donald Trump plans to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, in addition to their already scheduled three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. A U.S. official confirmed the Trump-Putin meeting, which will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting. Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin in their joint meeting about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia's invasion. Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin as relations between the United States and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.

Trump landed in China on Wednesday seeking to reinforce America's status as the world's leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left his administration scrambling to calm the U.S. public. The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty before the meeting with Xi and Putin. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump's behalf, stating there was "zero" evidence that the outages were connected or tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill reports that the meeting is drawing comparisons to the Yalta Conference and that Trump is on the opposite side of Xi and Putin in the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, though he has played down their support for Tehran. The Free Press includes a segment about the technical outages and mentions a report from CNN about Iran developing plans to deploy a dirty bomb in Washington, D.C. FOX News states that the meeting is a "two versus one" scenario with China and Russia working together against Trump, and that China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine. Al Jazeera and Newsweek focus on the nuclear disarmament agenda, with Newsweek noting that China's nuclear stockpile is growing and that Beijing may not be interested in reducing its arsenal. The Hill and Newsweek both mention the U.S. Defense Department's estimate that China's nuclear warhead count is likely to exceed 1,000 by the end of the decade.

Sources NPR · The Hill · The Free Press · FOX News · Al Jazeera · Newsweek

No source labeled left covered this story.

Anthropic raises over $100 billion in record-setting IPO

Anthropic, an artificial intelligence company, raised more than $100 billion in its initial public offering (IPO), setting a new record. The company, which was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers, is valued at around $1.5 trillion. The IPO, which includes the sale of 956 million shares at $83 each, is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. Anthropic's revenue in the first half of 2026 surged 1,300% to $16.3 billion, with adjusted operating income reaching $1.6 billion. The company also plans to raise an additional $26 billion through private placements with tech giants like Google, Microsoft, and Nvidia.

The IPO comes amid growing concerns about an AI bubble, with investors wary of the sector's volatility. Despite these concerns, the IPO is seen as a significant milestone for the AI industry, with some analysts predicting the stock could rise sharply on its first day of trading. Anthropic's rapid growth and dominance in the AI market have positioned it as a key player in the ongoing competition with companies like OpenAI and Meta.

Where the accounts differ

NPR states that Anthropic raised more than $107 billion, while Al Jazeera reports $81.3 billion. CBS News mentions $107 billion as well but notes that the total haul is more than $107 billion, which conflicts with Al Jazeera's figure. Axios and BBC do not specify the exact amount raised, focusing instead on broader implications and market context. The discrepancy in the total amount raised is attributed to different sources and reporting methods.

Sources NPR · CBS News · Axios · BBC · Al Jazeera · Mother Jones

House Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House

House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries as their nominee for speaker of the House in a closed-door vote, with 251 yes votes and 11 no votes. Jeffries, a Brooklyn native and current House minority leader, is set to become the first Black speaker of the House if he secures the required 218 votes in January. The vote followed a blue wave that gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress. Jeffries emphasized the economy and affordability as central to his leadership, vowing to fight for every American and challenge the status quo. Other historic leadership choices included Rep. Katherine Clark becoming the first woman to serve as majority leader and Rep. Pete Aguilar becoming the first Latino majority whip.

Jeffries faced opposition from a group of progressive Democrats, including Rep.-elects Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Frederick Haynes, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Chris Rabb, and Claire Valdez, who stated they voted no because they believe the party's direction does not fully reflect constituent demands. These members cited issues such as Medicare for All, ending the war in Israel, and reforming immigration policies as priorities. Jeffries also faced criticism from some members for his support of Israel and ties to corporate political action committees.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and NPR both state that Jeffries received 251 yes votes and 11 no votes, while FOX News and the New York Post report the same numbers. However, FOX News and the New York Post mention that two members did not vote, whereas ABC News and NPR do not. The New York Post and FOX News note that Jeffries requested a tallied vote, while ABC News and NPR state he requested a recorded vote. The New York Post and FOX News also mention that Jeffries changed his approach to follow the 2018 model, while ABC News and NPR do not. The New York Post and FOX News report that Rep.-elect Don Leonard was threatened by senior Democrats if he voted no, a detail not included in ABC News or NPR.

Sources ABC News · Axios · NPR · BBC · FOX News · New York Post

Duffy's $50 billion request gets chilly reception from Senate GOP

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is seeking $50 billion in additional funding to overhaul the nation's air traffic control system, a request that has drawn skepticism from Senate Republicans. The funding request follows a nationwide ground stop that disrupted over 18,000 flights and caused nearly 28,000 delays. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford stated that the disruption was caused by a newly installed router in El Dorado, Arkansas, and that no evidence of foul play or AI involvement was found. The FAA is currently relying on older Cisco routers to maintain operations while investigating the cause.

Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford pitched the funding request to Senate Republicans at their weekly lunch, with some lawmakers questioning whether the full $50 billion is necessary. Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz suggested using the fast-track reconciliation process to secure additional funds but emphasized the need to demonstrate effective use of the $12.5 billion already allocated. Senate Majority Leader John Thune expressed concerns about unspent funds and preferred working with Democrats through the normal appropriations process. Democrats also expressed skepticism, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer noting that Duffy and the FAA must show they can effectively implement the funding.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that Sen. John Kennedy criticized Duffy for initially requesting $30 billion and then increasing the ask to $50 billion, suggesting Duffy may have been taking orders. The Daily Wire states that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy linked the ground stop to routine maintenance performed by L3Harris. ABC News notes that Duffy increased his funding request from $30 billion to $50 billion after the ground stop, citing a need for a "massive portion of the needs of the airspace." NPR and The Hill mention that Duffy's request has drawn criticism for lacking a detailed plan, with Sen. Jack Reed and Rep. Rosa DeLauro questioning the justification for the additional $50 billion.

Sources Axios · The Daily Wire · The Dispatch · ABC News · NPR · The Hill

No source labeled left covered this story.

House Dems target Trump family, JD Vance in sweeping new investigation push

House Democrats, led by Rep. Robert Garcia, have sent document preservation letters to 12 figures in President Donald Trump's orbit, including Vice President JD Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle, and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. The letters, part of preparations for investigations in the new Congress, focus on the Trump family's business dealings, alleged misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and the federal government's handling of Jeffrey Epstein's case. Garcia described the probes as laying the groundwork for legislation to help all Americans.

The White House has warned that Democrats' use of oversight powers could constitute criminal behavior, with White House Counsel Will Scharf joining 'Fox News Sunday' to address the threats. The administration has also criticized the investigations as politically motivated, with White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis stating that Democrats are choosing to work against the American people if they pursue "sham investigations and radical left policies."

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that the letters to Trump's eldest sons include claims that they have "engaged in business pursuits that appear to have allowed you to personally profit from your father’s presidency on a massive scale and at the expense of the American people." NPR and New York Post also include similar language in their letters. Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire provide more specific financial figures, such as the $1.4 billion from World Liberty Financial and the $236 million from token sales. Slate does not mention specific financial figures or the Trump family's business dealings, focusing instead on broader themes of accountability and institutional reform.

Sources FOX News · NPR · Washington Examiner · New York Post · The Daily Wire · Slate

Photos Show Damage to $60M US Military Aircraft As Irish National Charged

Federal prosecutors have charged an Irish national with destroying a U.S. military aircraft after he allegedly broke into a U.S. Air National Guard C-130H at Shannon Airport and caused damage that left the $60 million plane unable to return to active flight. The indictment against Daithí O’Corrain, also known as David Curran, includes photos of damage to the aircraft’s cockpit and exterior. Prosecutors allege that O’Corrain cut wiring and hydraulic lines, smashed cockpit gauges, punctured air ducts and brought gallium onto the plane. They say he also struck the aircraft with an axe and put objects, including ball bearings, into its fuel tanks. The U.S. charge is destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison if he is convicted. O’Corrain is also facing proceedings in Ireland over the April incident.

The incident is described as part of a pattern of security breaches at Shannon Airport, which is a transatlantic hub for U.S. military personnel and equipment. Prosecutors cite three incidents in 2025 involving other people, including a van breach on May 1, paint-spraying on a U.S. military aircraft on May 17, and a van breach on November 22. The indictment also mentions that O’Corrain planned the attack for months, researching the aircraft and airport, acquiring tools and gallium, and using an app to track aircraft movements.

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek and The Guardian both mention that O’Corrain was arrested by Irish law enforcement officers, while FOX News and the New York Post describe him as being "nabbed by Irish authorities shortly after." The Guardian and ABC News state that O’Corrain is not in U.S. custody and his arraignment has not been scheduled, whereas the New York Post claims he is being held at an Irish prison. The Guardian and ABC News also mention an online fundraiser organized by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends, which the other accounts do not. The New York Post refers to O’Corrain as an "independent peace activist," a characterization not present in the other accounts. The Washington Examiner and FOX News both refer to O’Corrain as an "anti-Israel activist," while the Guardian and ABC News do not make this claim.

Sources Newsweek · Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Guardian · ABC News · New York Post

Iran launches a third round of strikes on Bahrain, host of U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet

Iran fired drones at a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain on Tuesday, marking the third such attack in five days, according to multiple outlets. The U.S. military confirmed that its air defense systems intercepted the drones without causing damage to equipment or injury to personnel. The strikes followed a two-month lull in hostilities between Iran and the U.S. In response, the U.S. conducted a strike on an Iranian missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz, using precision munitions. The attack was described as a self-defense measure against Iranian aggression. Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, reported that its air defenses successfully intercepted the Iranian aerial attacks. The U.S. military also noted that the attack on Bahrain did not result in damage to its assets.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and The Hill both report that Iran launched three attacks on U.S. targets in Bahrain in five days, with the U.S. military confirming no damage or casualties. FOX News and BBC, however, mention that the attack on Kuwait was the first in two months, with Kuwait repelling the attack. CBS News does not mention the attacks on Bahrain or Kuwait, focusing instead on the broader energy crisis and Trump's comments on Iran's potential biological weapons. The Hill and FOX News differ on the timing of the U.S. strike, with The Hill stating it occurred after a two-month pause, while FOX News reports it as a response to Iran's attacks. NPR and BBC both attribute the U.S. strike to self-defense, while FOX News and The Hill also mention the strike as a response to Iranian aggression.

Sources NPR · The Hill · FOX News · BBC · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Ukraine's strike on the Kerch bridge disrupts Russian military supply lines, potentially altering the course of the war in Crimea and threatening regional stability.

Ukraine strikes Crimean Bridge, damaging key Russian supply route

Ukrainian forces launched a coordinated attack on the Kerch Bridge, a critical link between Russia and occupied Crimea, using a combination of drones and missiles. The attack, which occurred over several days, resulted in significant damage to the bridge’s road section, with a large portion collapsing into the sea. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the operation as “unprecedented,” noting it had been planned over weeks. The strike disrupted rail and road traffic, with Russia confirming temporary suspensions of train services. The bridge, built in 2018, has been a frequent target for Kyiv, with previous attacks in 2022 and 2023 causing partial damage. The latest strike is part of Ukraine’s broader strategy to isolate Crimea from Russia, though a complete blockade remains elusive.

The attack involved multiple stages, including the use of drones to disable Russian air defenses and a relay system for real-time communication. Ukrainian military sources indicated the operation was designed to send a message to global leaders, particularly ahead of a trilateral summit between Putin, Trump, and Xi Jinping. The bridge, which Putin personally opened in 2018, is seen as a symbol of Russian dominance and has been repeatedly targeted by Kyiv as part of its efforts to undermine Moscow’s military logistics.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the attack was part of a “seventh stage of an operation” and that the bridge was damaged in a multi-stage plan involving drones and missiles. FOX News states that the attack destroyed one of the bridge’s two steel arches and the road span, with footage showing half the bridge missing. Newsweek mentions that the attack occurred just before a meeting between Trump and Putin, and that the bridge was struck for the third time in a week. The BBC describes the attack as a “seven-stage operation” that culminated in the collapse of the road arch, with a verified video showing the missile strike. The Guardian also notes that the bridge was previously damaged in 2022 and 2023, while FOX News and Newsweek provide details on the extent of the damage and the involvement of specific weapons like the FP-5 Flamingo missile. The BBC and The Guardian differ in their descriptions of the bridge’s structural impact, with the BBC emphasizing the catastrophic nature of the damage and the difficulty of rebuilding.

Sources The Guardian · FOX News · Newsweek · BBC

No source labeled lean-left or lean-right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Inside the Fight to Bring Jensen Huang Back to Nvidia

Jensen Huang, former CEO of Nvidia, resigned last week over multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving Alice Huang, a woman identified by US intelligence as a possible spy for the Chinese government. A campaign called “Bring Jensen Back” has gathered nearly 180,000 signatures, urging Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang while an independent investigation establishes the facts. The campaign includes signatories such as Elon Musk and Steve Chen, along with current and former Nvidia employees. The FBI has been investigating Huang’s affair with Alice Huang for at least a year. Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, has been managing the company’s shift to AI-focused chipmaking. President Trump has expressed support for Huang’s potential return, stating he “would not mind” if Huang were reinstated as CEO.

The campaign argues that Huang deserves due process and fairness, emphasizing his long-standing contributions to the company. It claims that the company’s future is not the main concern of those pushing for Huang’s return, but rather a sense of appreciation for his work. The campaign states that Huang “poured his heart and soul into building NVIDIA” and that the company “is the work of his life.” The campaign also highlights that the tech industry is “primarily led by men, designed by men, and is far more likely to be used by men.”

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones reports that the FBI has been investigating Huang’s affair with Alice Huang for at least a year, while The Daily Wire states that the FBI investigation began after the affair was revealed. The Daily Wire also claims that Alice Huang was a former television journalist who later worked at Megaspeed, a detail not mentioned in Mother Jones. The Daily Wire attributes the claim that Megaspeed purchased over $4 billion in Nvidia hardware to its own reporting, while Mother Jones does not specify the amount. The Free Press does not mention the affair or the campaign to reinstate Huang, focusing instead on Trump’s meeting with Xi and Putin.

Sources Mother Jones · The Hill · FOX News · The Daily Wire · BBC · The Free Press

Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?

Democratic candidate Mary Peltola has won the US Senate race in Alaska, beating Republican incumbent Senator Dan S Sullivan to complete the Democrats' sweeping victory in the midterm elections. Peltola sealed the win after reaching 50.1% with 99% of votes counted - making Alaska the last Senate seat to be called after the 3 November election. Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices are used to decide who wins.

The race was complicated by the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan. Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term. Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign. The New York Times reported that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr. Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign. President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank, while NPR states that Peltola won a majority of Alaskans' first-place votes, meaning no ranked-choice calculation was needed. Al Jazeera mentions that the Trump administration alleged that Peltola’s campaign had deliberately recruited the second Dan Sullivan to divide Republican votes, while ABC News states that the Department of Justice preemptively sued to block the certification of the election if Dan S Sullivan lost. Axios highlights that Peltola's victory was driven by support in four Alaska Native strongholds, while Newsweek notes that James Comer claimed Peltola could still face legal challenges over her victory.

Sources BBC · NPR · Al Jazeera · ABC News · Axios · Newsweek

Chuck Schumer Faces Leadership Challenge from Chris Van Hollen

Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, faced criticism for his election night speech following Democrats' midterm victories, which some argued failed to address key issues like the Iran War and tech influence. His remarks were seen as out of touch with current concerns, prompting calls for leadership change. Senate Minority Leader Chris Van Hollen, a progressive Democrat from Maryland, has emerged as a challenger to Schumer's leadership, arguing that the party needs a new direction. Van Hollen emphasized the need for more inclusive decision-making and highlighted the importance of addressing issues like the war in Iran and military aid to Israel. He also pointed to the success of progressive candidates like Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan as evidence of a shift in Democratic priorities.

Van Hollen's campaign for leadership has gained traction, with him appearing on major networks to outline his vision for the party. He claims the midterm elections were a populist rejection of Trump, not a Washington-driven victory. Van Hollen also called for an end to U.S. funding for the Iran War and criticized Schumer's continued support for military aid to Israel despite his criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Where the accounts differ

The Nation reports that Schumer's speech omitted key issues like the Iran War and tech influence, while NPR and ABC News do not mention this omission. The Nation attributes Schumer's criticism of Republicans to a focus on "extraneous things" and "costs, chaos, and corruption," whereas NPR and ABC News do not include this specific phrasing. The Nation also notes that Schumer's metaphor about the "red brick wall" was confusing, a detail not present in NPR or ABC News. NPR and ABC News do not mention the Nation's characterization of Schumer as a "political dinosaur."

Sources The Nation · NPR · ABC News · Axios · Washington Examiner · The Daily Caller

US intel detects Iranian dirty bomb plot targeting Washington: reports

U.S. intelligence officials have reportedly detected a plot by Iran to detonate a dirty bomb in Washington, D.C., according to multiple outlets. The intelligence includes specific locations and potential targets, prompting contingency planning by American officials. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis stated that there are "no credible threats to the homeland" at this time. President Trump has said the administration is taking the report "very seriously" and warned Iran would face "unprecedented retaliation" if it attacked the U.S. The intelligence reportedly includes intercepted Iranian communications suggesting bomb-making materials had been stashed inside the U.S. However, officials remain divided over the credibility of these claims and whether Iran has the personnel to execute such an attack.

Iran has denied the allegations, with its Foreign Ministry calling the claims "baseless." The report also mentions that Iran has previously been linked to plots targeting Americans on U.S. soil, including a 2011 plot to assassinate Saudi Arabia’s ambassador and a 2024 plot to assassinate Trump. The intelligence suggests that radioactive material or chemical agents needed for the dirty bomb may have been stashed in the U.S. for years, and that Iran could have used the "porous" border to bring in operatives. The White House has reportedly held several meetings to discuss potential countermeasures, though no public confirmation exists that Iran has positioned materials or operatives for an attack.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and The Daily Wire both mention that U.S. officials have been meeting to discuss the intelligence, but The Daily Wire adds that the White House pushed back on the assessment, calling the reported planning "aspirational." The Washington Examiner notes that Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed the reports as not indicating an "imminent threat," while the New York Post states that officials are "divided over how credible the intelligence is." The Daily Wire and FOX News both include quotes from Iran’s Foreign Ministry denying the allegations, but FOX News adds that Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi invoked Iran’s history as a victim of chemical warfare, which is not mentioned in the other accounts. The Daily Wire also includes details about the Secret Service moving Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent into military housing, which is not mentioned in the other accounts.

Sources New York Post · The Daily Wire · BBC · FOX News · Axios · Washington Examiner

No source labeled left covered this story.

White House withdraws Heidi Overton’s nomination to become next FDA commissioner

The White House has withdrawn Heidi Overton’s nomination to become the next Food and Drug Administration commissioner before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee was due to consider her on Wednesday. Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was nominated by President Trump in August. The decision comes the day before the Senate's Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee was scheduled to vote on her nomination. The FDA has been led by acting commissioner Kyle Diamantas since Marty Makary resigned in May.

Overton faced skepticism from some Republicans over her role in the administration's efforts to change childhood vaccine recommendations. A senior administration official told Axios that Overton did not have enough support to be confirmed as the next FDA commissioner. The official stated, "We need to go in a new direction at FDA, and everybody fully supports [Health] Secretary [Robert F.] Kennedy Jr.'s vision to Make America Healthy Again and get back to a more populist and common-sense approach to health in America."

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and Just The News both state that the White House pulled the nomination due to lack of congressional support, while the New York Post and Axios attribute the withdrawal to bipartisan pushback and criticism over Overton's role in changing childhood vaccine recommendations. The New York Post and FOX News mention Overton's alleged "big tobacco ties" and anti-abortion stance, which are not included in the Washington Examiner or Just The News accounts. The FOX News account also includes details about Overton's confirmation hearing and her clashes with Senator Bernie Sanders and Senator Bill Cassidy, which are not present in the other accounts. The CBS News account adds information about Overton's testimony regarding the FDA-approved chemical abortion drug mifepristone and her execution of Trump's pro-vaping policies, which are not mentioned in the other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · Just The News · FOX News · CBS News · Axios · New York Post

New York City Mayor Disbands NYPD Counterterrorism Unit Amid Protests and Civilian Oversight Plans

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Monday that he would dissolve the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group (SRG), a unit responsible for counterterrorism and managing protest crowds. The SRG was formed in 2015. Mamdani stated that the move fulfills a campaign promise to separate counterterrorism from protest response. The city plans to replace the SRG with a civilian-led “Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division” and a “First Amendment Support Team,” both of which will lack weapons and arrest powers. The NYPD will also create a new Patrol Support Division with officers trained in crowd management. The reforms include banning irritant gas, kettling, and long guns during protests. The NYPD’s intelligence and counterterrorism functions will be consolidated within the department’s intelligence bureau.

The New York Post reported that the SRG was involved in incidents such as the June 2020 kettling of protesters, the Gracie Mansion bombing attempt, and the NFL Headquarters mass shooting. The Guardian noted that the SRG has faced criticism for using excessive force and aggressive tactics against protesters, and that the reforms include significant restrictions on police tactics during demonstrations.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and The Guardian differ in the specific incidents cited involving the SRG. The New York Post mentions the June 2020 kettling incident, the Gracie Mansion bombing attempt, and the NFL Headquarters mass shooting, while The Guardian does not include these specific events. The Guardian also notes that the SRG has faced criticism for using excessive force, while The New York Post attributes this criticism to civil rights groups. The Free Press and FOX News do not provide specific incidents, focusing instead on the broader implications of the SRG’s dissolution. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller attribute the SRG’s role in preventing violence to its counterterrorism capabilities, while The Guardian and The New York Post emphasize the unit’s involvement in protest management.

Sources New York Post · The Guardian · The Free Press · FOX News · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump

A Pakistani man, Asif Merchant, was sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in an Iran-backed plot to assassinate former U.S. President Donald Trump. Merchant was found guilty in March of attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and murder for hire. The plot involved hiring hitmen to kill Trump, former President Joe Biden, and former U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley. The hitmen were undercover FBI agents. Merchant claimed he acted under the direction of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to avenge the 2020 U.S. airstrike that killed Iranian general Qasem Soleimani. He was arrested in July 2024 in Texas as he prepared to leave the U.S. The sentence was handed down by U.S. District Judge Eric R. Komitee.

Prosecutors stated that Merchant traveled to Iran 15 times, where he received training from Iranian intelligence officers, before coming to the U.S. in April 2024. He paid $5,000 to the undercover hitmen as an initial payment. The Department of Justice described the IRGC as a global terrorist force. Merchant admitted to being recruited by the IRGC in 2022 and said he was forced into the plot to protect his family in Iran.

Where the accounts differ

BBC and The Guardian both report that Merchant was arrested in July 2024 in Texas, while The Daily Wire and Just The News state he was arrested on July 12, 2024. CBS News mentions that Merchant was arrested on July 12, 2024, the day before Thomas Matthew Crooks shot Trump during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. The Daily Wire and The Guardian note that Merchant had searched for Trump rally locations and used Google Maps to find a rally in New Jersey, while BBC and CBS News do not mention this detail. The Daily Wire and The Guardian also state that Merchant had social media posts praising Soleimani, which BBC and CBS News do not mention. The Washington Examiner does not mention the arrest date or the Google Maps activity.

Sources BBC · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · Just The News · CBS News · The Guardian

Clarence Thomas calls foul on California ruling he says could turn citizens into government mouthpieces

The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge to California’s requirement that licensed physicians complete continuing medical education (CME) courses including discussion of implicit bias. The case involves Dr. Azadeh Khatibi, a physician who argues the state compels her to convey a government-favored message in violation of the First Amendment. California maintains that while instructors must include discussion of implicit bias, they are not required to personally endorse the theory and may openly disagree with it. The Ninth Circuit previously ruled that CME courses constitute government speech due to California’s extensive regulation of the medical profession, meaning the state’s requirements are not subject to First Amendment scrutiny.

Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Samuel Alito, dissented from the Supreme Court’s decision not to take up the case. They argued that California’s implicit-bias-training requirement compels instructors to affirm the state’s view that implicit bias causes disparities in health outcomes, thereby violating First Amendment protections. Thomas warned that allowing the law to stand could have implications beyond the medical field, potentially enabling states to compel speech from private citizens.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and FOX News both report that Thomas and Alito dissented from the Supreme Court’s decision not to take up the case, and that they argued California’s law compels private speakers to communicate the government’s viewpoint. The New York Post adds that Thomas and Alito said the Ninth Circuit erred in finding that the CME requirement is government speech. FOX News omits this specific critique and instead reports that Thomas and Alito disputed California’s characterization of whether it was compelling instructors to take certain positions. The Axios and ABC News accounts do not mention the dissenting justices’ specific arguments about the government-speech doctrine, focusing instead on the broader context of the Supreme Court’s decision on DEI-related issues.

Sources New York Post · Axios · ABC News · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: US sanctions on ICJ judges could undermine international justice for Myanmar genocide victims, jeopardizing rights of Rohingya refugees.

Fears grow over US sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is set to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. The US has warned that it may impose sanctions on ICJ judges, including Nobel peace prize winner Navi Pillay, if the court finds Myanmar guilty. The US and Israel fear the ruling could set a precedent that makes it easier to accuse other states of genocide. Lawyers for Rohingya survivors argue that Myanmar’s military actions in 2016 and 2017 show clear intent to destroy the Rohingya group. The US has already sanctioned ICC judges and called the ICC a “rogue court.” The Gambia, as a litigant, appointed Pillay as an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar.

Rohingya refugees, including Dil Hossain and his family, have fled Myanmar and now live in refugee camps in Bangladesh. They hope the ICJ ruling will recognize the atrocities against the Rohingya and support their return home. Over 1.2 million Rohingya remain in Bangladesh, many in camps in Cox’s Bazar. Despite the legal case, the prospects for a safe return are uncertain due to ongoing conflict in Myanmar. Rohingya refugees describe life in exile as marked by hardship, dependence on aid, and mental distress.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the US and Israel fear the ICJ ruling could set a precedent for accusing other states of genocide, including Israel in Gaza. It also mentions that the US has sanctioned ICC judges and called the ICC a “rogue court.” The Guardian attributes the claim about the US warning judges to Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, and quotes him directly. Al Jazeera does not mention the US-Israel concern or the sanctions against the ICC. Al Jazeera focuses on the personal stories of Rohingya refugees and their hopes for justice, while The Guardian emphasizes the political and legal implications of the ruling.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera

No source labeled center or lean-right or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

FAA Ground Stop Blamed on Router Overload and Copper Wire Replacement

On November 13, 2026, a nationwide FAA ground stop stranded hundreds of thousands of airline travelers. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy attributed the incident to a router overload caused by the replacement of copper wire with fiber-optic cable in El Dorado, Arkansas. He stated that the router in question was broadcasting data into the national airspace network, leading to system instability. The ground stop lasted over four hours, with flights resuming by 8:15 p.m. Friday. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford confirmed that the system was stable post-ground stop and that no lives were at risk. Duffy also called for additional congressional funding to complete the FAA modernization, which includes replacing all copper wiring by the end of 2028.

Duffy emphasized that the issue was not a cyberattack but rather a technical problem with the aging air traffic control system. He noted that the FAA had spent approximately 38% of the $12.5 billion allocated for modernization, with an additional $10.1 billion needed to complete the project. During a press conference, Duffy mentioned that the router in question was being investigated at an L3Harris lab in Florida, and that the issue may have originated from either user error or a faulty installation.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones reports that Duffy blamed previous administrations for a lack of investment, citing 30 years of underfunding. ABC News states that Duffy attributed the issue to a router in Arkansas and that the problem was being investigated with the FBI. CBS News, however, focuses on unrelated bank outages and does not mention the FAA incident. The Hill highlights Duffy’s $50 billion funding request and mentions that Democrats are skeptical of the request. The Christian Science Monitor details the number of canceled flights and the impact on travelers. Washington Examiner notes that Mullin cited an unnamed expert blaming AI for the outages, a claim not mentioned by other outlets.

Sources Mother Jones · ABC News · CBS News · The Hill · Christian Science Monitor · Washington Examiner

Bessent: Nvidia should ‘go outside the company’ for next CEO

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Nvidia’s board to seek a new CEO from outside the company, citing the need for a dramatic shake-up following former CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. Bessent made the remarks during an interview with Larry Kudlow, emphasizing that while Huang is a “wonderful innovator,” the company must prioritize compliance. Huang stepped down after admitting to an affair with an employee and being accused of espionage.

President Donald Trump is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a high-stakes Asia trip, bringing along two Cabinet officials with differing views on China’s access to U.S. AI technology. Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are accompanying Trump, despite reports of a dispute over whether to blacklist a company suspected of aiding China in obtaining restricted Nvidia chips.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and FOX News both mention Bessent’s call for a dramatic shake-up at Nvidia, but only the Washington Examiner attributes this to a direct quote from Bessent. FOX News also reports that Bessent confirmed several departments supported adding Megaspeed to the Commerce Department’s Entity List, a claim not present in the Washington Examiner. The Daily Wire notes that Trump left the door open to raising the Huang scandal with Xi, a detail absent from the other accounts. NPR and ABC News do not mention the Huang scandal in the context of the Asia trip, while Axios focuses on the broader implications of the Huang resignation for the AI industry.

Sources Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Daily Wire · NPR · ABC News · Axios

Sen.-elect Scott Colom undecided in Van Hollen-Schumer race: ‘I’m in listening mode’

Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D-MS) has not yet decided whether to support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) or Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) in their race to lead the Democratic caucus next year. Colom stated on NBC’s Meet the Press that he is in “listening mode,” emphasizing the need to understand the needs of the caucus and the leadership capabilities of his colleagues. Van Hollen, meanwhile, has asserted that he has a “path” to victory in his bid to oust Schumer, citing support and openness to change within the Senate Democratic caucus. Van Hollen also accused Schumer’s team of trying to instill fear among senators by leaking a list of committed voters for Schumer.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner reports that Colom is in “listening mode” and cites a senator who suggested this approach. The Guardian and ABC News both mention Van Hollen’s claim of having a “path” to victory, but the Guardian adds that Van Hollen accused Schumer’s team of leaking a list of supporters and attempting to intimidate senators. The Daily Wire and The Guardian also note that Van Hollen criticized Schumer’s team for trying to change the election date, while the Washington Examiner does not mention this claim. The Free Press and New York Post do not cover the Van Hollen-Schumer race, focusing instead on other political developments.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · ABC News · The Free Press · New York Post

Russia downs over 1,400 Ukrainian drones as Kyiv hits a key bridge in Crimea

Ukraine launched a major drone attack on Russia, with Russian air defenses reporting the downing of over 1,400 drones during the night. The attack coincided with Ukraine targeting a key bridge in Crimea, the Kerch Bridge, which connects the peninsula to mainland Russia. Russian officials confirmed that the bridge was struck again, leading to the suspension of traffic. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the strike as an "unprecedented operation" in response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. The attack also included the use of cruise missiles, according to Zelenskyy.

The Kerch Bridge, a critical supply route for Russian military and civilian traffic, was hit for the second consecutive day. Russian-installed authorities in Crimea reported damage to the bridge, though the extent was unclear. Ukrainian officials claimed the attack caused significant damage, including the collapse of one of the bridge's arches. The strike is seen as a symbolic blow to Russian President Vladimir Putin, especially ahead of an upcoming trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and Al Jazeera both report that Russia downed 1,441 drones on Tuesday, while ABC News and The Daily Wire cite Russia's Defense Ministry as reporting 1,441 drones on Tuesday and 1,484 drones from Sunday night through Monday. FOX News reports Russia intercepted 1,336 drones on Monday, which is lower than the numbers reported by other outlets. Al Jazeera and ABC News mention that the Kerch Bridge was hit for the second consecutive day, while FOX News and The Daily Wire state that the bridge was struck for the second time in 18 months and that the damage was described as minor by the Kremlin. Newsweek and ABC News describe the bridge as partially collapsing, while NPR and Al Jazeera do not specify the extent of the damage.

Sources NPR · Al Jazeera · ABC News · Newsweek · FOX News · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Lindsay Clancy Is Headed Back To Court As Judge Sets Retrial Date

Lindsay Clancy, 36, will face a second murder trial for the deaths of her three children, Cora (5), Dawson (3), and Callan (8 months), following a mistrial in her first trial. A Massachusetts judge, William Sullivan, set jury selection for March 29, 2027, with pre-trial hearings scheduled for late December and February 18, 2027. Prosecutors from Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz’s office confirmed they would proceed with the case, though they did not explicitly state the charges. Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, interpreted the prosecution’s push for a jury trial as an indication that first-degree murder charges would be pursued again.

The first trial ended in a mistrial on September 4, 2026, after a jury deadlocked 11-1. The defense had previously sought to have the holdout juror removed and to dismiss the case on double jeopardy grounds, but those motions were denied. Clancy’s attorneys argued she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings and should not be held criminally responsible.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and FOX News both mention that prosecutors did not explicitly declare first-degree murder charges, but Reddington interpreted their push for a jury trial as an indication of intent to proceed with first-degree charges. The Daily Wire and BBC note that the district attorney has not officially confirmed the charges, while FOX News and The Daily Caller state that prosecutors did not specifically address whether they intended to seek the same charges. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller mention that Sullivan pushed for a mid-March trial date, while FOX News and NPR note that prosecutors had initially wanted a May trial date.

Sources The Daily Wire · NPR · BBC · FOX News · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Robert Pattinson Announced as New James Bond

The James Bond franchise has officially announced Robert Pattinson as its next 007. Pattinson, known for roles in "The Batman," "Twilight," and "Harry Potter," will take over from Daniel Craig, who retired after "No Time to Die" in 2021. The new film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, who previously worked with Pattinson on the "Dune" franchise. The film will be the 26th Bond movie and the first under Amazon MGM's creative control since they acquired the franchise in 2025.

Pattinson expressed his excitement about the role, calling it "a dream come true." He stated that the franchise has "the timeless soul of 007" and that he is "overjoyed" to join the project. The British royal family responded to the news on social media, welcoming Pattinson to "His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr. Bond." The announcement ended months of speculation about who would succeed Craig, with fans debating potential candidates like Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, and Nicholas Hoult.

Where the accounts differ

The Free Press and The Daily Wire both describe the selection of Pattinson as the new Bond, but The Free Press emphasizes the cultural significance of the Bond character across different eras, while The Daily Wire focuses on the literary roots of the Bond character and criticizes recent film adaptations for straying from Ian Fleming's original novels. CBS News and The Daily Caller provide more detailed information about the casting process, including the screen tests and the involvement of Steven Knight as the screenwriter. The Daily Wire also mentions Barbara Broccoli's comments on the gender of the next Bond, which is not included in the other accounts.

Sources The Free Press · CBS News · The Daily Wire · Slate · The Daily Caller

White House Counsel Warns Democrats Against Abuse Of Oversight Power

White House Counsel Will Scharf warned Democratic lawmakers against using congressional oversight powers for purposes other than legitimate legislative tasks. In a letter to Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming House Oversight Committee chair, Scharf accused Democrats of making "abusive and capricious threats" against the White House. Scharf also told Fox News that Democrats' intent to investigate the Trump administration was "out of pettiness."

Scharf instructed all executive branch agencies to obtain White House approval before allowing any employee to testify before Congress. This directive was outlined in a memo obtained by Axios and reported by Just The News. The memo emphasizes that investigations must serve a "legitimate legislative purpose" and not be used for "self-aggrandizement" or to "punish" those investigated.

The White House official described the administration's stance as resisting "politically motivated baseless investigations," while also expressing readiness to engage with Congress on reasonable requests.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Caller reports that Scharf called Garcia's threats "shocking" and accused him of making "abusive and capricious threats" against the White House. Axios and Just The News do not mention Scharf calling Garcia's statements "shocking." The Daily Caller also includes a direct quote from Garcia in which he says, "We’re not going to be intimidated by the president," which is not included in the other accounts. Washington Examiner does not mention the specific quote from Garcia or the characterization of his statements as "shocking."

Sources The Daily Caller · Axios · Just The News · Washington Examiner

No source labeled left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: An illegal migrant accused of attempted murder remains at large after being released from Rikers Island despite an ICE detainer, endangering public safety and highlighting flaws in immigration enforcement.

Illegal migrant accused of attempted murder at large after Rikers release despite ICE detainer: DHS

A Guyanese citizen living in the United States illegally remains at large after being released from custody in New York City earlier this month, despite facing multiple violent felony charges and an active federal immigration detainer, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Delon Raymond Jaundoo was arrested in Brooklyn on charges including attempted murder, first- and second-degree assault, criminal use of a firearm, and multiple counts of criminal possession of a loaded weapon. His prior criminal record also includes an arrest for third-degree assault. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged an immigration detainer for Jaundoo on April 29, which the New York City Department of Correction declined to honor, allowing him to be released from Rikers Island.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin criticized New York’s sanctuary policies following the release, arguing that state and local laws prevent cooperation with federal immigration authorities even in cases involving violent offenses. Jaundoo lawfully entered the country during the Obama administration but overstayed his authorized stay, which expired in January 2015, according to DHS. Jaundoo’s release comes amid ongoing restrictions on local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. Upon taking office, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed an executive order limiting city coordination with ICE, and a state law signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul took effect in August barring local authorities from cooperating with federal immigration officials.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post states that DHS officials stated Jaundoo lawfully entered the country during the Obama administration but overstayed his authorized stay, which expired in January 2015. FOX News does not include this detail about Jaundoo’s entry and overstaying. The New York Post also mentions that a spokesperson for Hochul told Fox News Digital that “Governor Hochul has been clear: New York State is not and never will be a sanctuary for violent criminals,” while FOX News includes this quote but does not attribute it to a spokesperson for Hochul. The New York Post notes that DHS stated several other illegal immigrants arrested for or convicted of violent crimes have similarly been released from custody under the state’s current policies, while FOX News does not include this statement from DHS.

Sources New York Post · FOX News

No source labeled center or lean-left or lean-right or left covered this story.
