FAA Ground Stop Strands Travelers, Sparks Debate Over System Modernization

On November 13, 2026, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop, halting all departures across the U.S. due to a telecommunications outage. The stop, which lasted over four hours, stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers and disrupted air traffic. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy attributed the outage to an overloaded network caused by maintenance work by FAA contractor L3Harris, which was replacing copper wiring with fiber-optic cables. Duffy called for additional congressional funding to modernize the FAA’s system, which he said had been underfunded for decades. The FAA administrator, Bryan Bedford, confirmed that the system was stable after the ground stop and apologized for the disruption. President Trump also weighed in, urging Congress to approve more funding for air traffic control modernization.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and CBS News both report that Duffy claimed the FAA had spent 38% of the $12.5 billion allocated for modernization, while The Hill and Christian Science Monitor note that only one-third of the funds had been spent. The Hill and CBS News mention that the Trump administration had requested $50 billion for the FAA, while Mother Jones and FOX News report that the request was for $50 billion, with The Hill noting that the Trump administration had previously requested $30 billion. The Hill and Christian Science Monitor provide specific numbers on flight cancellations, while Mother Jones and CBS News do not. FOX News and The Hill attribute the outage to a communications failure, while CBS News and Mother Jones attribute it to overloaded routers caused by maintenance work.

Sources Mother Jones · The Hill · Washington Examiner · FOX News · CBS News · Christian Science Monitor

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid allegations of affairs and China spy ties

Jensen Huang, co-founder and former CEO of Nvidia, resigned abruptly after reports surfaced of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman suspected of espionage. The scandal has raised concerns about potential illegal chip exports to China, despite U.S. export restrictions. Huang's resignation followed a staff-wide memo admitting to the affair, which led to his immediate dismissal. Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO, was named interim CEO. The company faces scrutiny over its financial practices and the sustainability of the AI investment boom, with some analysts warning of a potential market correction. Meanwhile, a bipartisan push for tighter export controls on advanced chips to China has intensified, with calls for stricter oversight of companies like Megaspeed, a major Nvidia client.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that the AI investment bubble is at risk due to financial strain and political uncertainty, citing projections of $7 trillion in infrastructure spending versus $3.6 trillion in revenue. The BBC highlights the potential for high-end AI chips to reach China through Megaspeed, noting the company's internal investigation and its denial of wrongdoing. The New York Post and The Guardian both mention Scott Bessent's call for Nvidia to hire an external CEO, while The Guardian adds that Bessent prioritizes questions about chip sales to China over Huang's personal conduct. Fox Business notes the campaign for Huang's return, including support from Elon Musk and others, while The Hill states that Rep. Rick Crawford believes it is premature to blame Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for delays in export controls.

Sources Axios · BBC · New York Post · The Guardian · Fox Business · The Hill

Sen.-elect Scott Colom undecided in Van Hollen-Schumer race: ‘I’m in listening mode’

Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D-MS) has not yet decided which candidate to support in the race for Senate Democratic leadership between Chuck Schumer (D-NY) and Chris Van Hollen (D-MD). Colom stated he is in "listening mode" and emphasized the importance of understanding the needs of the caucus and identifying potential leaders. He cited a senator who suggested he focus on listening to colleagues, both familiar and unfamiliar, to determine the best course of action.

Chris Van Hollen has emerged as a challenger to Chuck Schumer, who has held the position of Senate minority leader since 2016 and became majority leader in 2021. Van Hollen has criticized Schumer for his March 2025 vote to advance a Republican-backed government funding bill, which some Democrats viewed as a missed opportunity to challenge President Trump’s policies. Van Hollen also argues that Schumer’s support for Israel has drawn criticism within the party, particularly regarding humanitarian concerns in Gaza.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner reports that Colom is undecided and in "listening mode," while The Daily Wire mentions that John Fetterman expressed concern about Van Hollen’s stance on Israel and suggested he might leave the party if Van Hollen is elected. The Free Press and The Daily Caller both mention Van Hollen’s challenge to Schumer, but The Free Press adds that Van Hollen has threatened to shut down the government to defund the war in Iran, a claim not present in other accounts. The ABC News account includes Van Hollen’s accusation that Schumer’s team is trying to instill fear among Democrats, a detail absent in other reports.

Sources Washington Examiner · Just The News · The Free Press · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · ABC News

At least 100 people pulled from Mississippi River after New Orleans ship crash as lengthy salvage effort looms

A tanker struck a docked cruise ship in New Orleans on Friday, resulting in over 100 people being rescued from the Mississippi River. Officials confirmed that everyone aboard the American Heritage cruise ship was accounted for, though eight people remained hospitalized, including two in serious condition. The U.S. Coast Guard is preparing for a potentially weeks-long operation to remove the capsized vessel, which will involve removing 16,000 gallons of fuel and assessing the vessel for potential hazardous material leaks. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has recovered the tanker's voyage data recorder and is expected to release a preliminary report within 30 days.

The Port of New Orleans filed a lawsuit seeking over $1 million in damages from the owner and operator of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker, alleging negligence in the collision. The lawsuit claims the tanker failed to take adequate precautions to avoid the collision, which caused significant damage to the port's terminal. The NTSB and Coast Guard are investigating the incident, with the exact cause remaining under review. The collision is described as a "miracle on the Mississippi" due to the survival of all passengers and crew.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that 191 passengers and crew were aboard the American Heritage, while The Guardian and CBS News state there were 129 passengers plus crew. The Guardian mentions that 32 people were hospitalized with non-critical injuries, while BBC and CBS News also note 32 people were hospitalized. The Guardian and BBC report that the American Heritage had 129 passengers, while FOX News and CBS News state there were 191 people aboard. The Guardian and BBC mention that the American Heritage was partially submerged, while FOX News and CBS News describe it as capsizing. The Guardian and BBC report that the Port of New Orleans filed a lawsuit, while FOX News and CBS News also mention the lawsuit but differ in the exact wording and details.

Sources FOX News · The Guardian · BBC · CBS News · Fox Business · New York Post

Iran claims drone attack on US radar in Bahrain; US intercepts drones

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it launched six drones at a US air defense radar system at Bahrain's Riffa Air Base in retaliation for what it described as "hostile US actions." The US military confirmed intercepting two Iranian drones on Friday but has not yet commented on Sunday's claim. Bahrain's authorities reported intercepting several aerial attacks and said no injuries or damage occurred. The IRGC also claimed that the Strait of Hormuz remains closed and that US efforts to escort ships through the waterway have failed.

Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken warned that a US ground invasion of Iran would be an "absolute disaster," citing the country's vast territory, population, and ability to produce weapons deep within its borders. Blinken emphasized that Iran's weapons capabilities are too deeply embedded for air power alone to neutralize. He also noted the geographic challenges of conducting a ground operation, including the long coastline along the Strait of Hormuz.

The attacks in Bahrain come amid ongoing tensions in Yemen, where Iran's Houthi allies have made advances against Saudi-backed forces. The IRGC also claimed that two oil tankers struck sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, though the US military has not confirmed these incidents. The US has conducted several strikes against Iranian targets in the region, including Qeshm Island, which Iran has condemned as an act of aggression.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that Blinken warned about a potential US ground invasion of Iran and attributed the claim about Iran's weapons production to his own statements. Washington Examiner and Al Jazeera do not mention Blinken's warning, focusing instead on the drone attacks in Bahrain. The Guardian includes details about the US strikes in Iran and the Houthi advances in Yemen, which are not covered in the other accounts. FOX News also mentions concerns in Iraq about the potential use of its territory for a US ground operation, which the other accounts do not address.

Sources FOX News · Washington Examiner · Al Jazeera · The Guardian

Two planes collide on taxiway at Miami airport one day after national grounding

Two planes collided with one another on a taxiway at Miami’s international airport on Saturday night – a day after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an hours-long nationwide ground stop due to communication issues affecting multiple air traffic control centers. The incident involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 and a United Parcel Service Boeing 767. Two people reportedly had minor injuries in the collision and subsequently received medical treatment. The FAA said it was investigating the matter, which was reported at about 9pm local time. Air traffic controllers had told the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight before the collision. The Copa flight was taxiing to the gate and the UPS flight was taxiing for departure to Bogotá, Colombia.

The collision happened at approximately 9:15 p.m., according to airport officials. Damage to the nose of the aircraft at Miami International Airport is seen in this photo. Photos showed damage to the nose of one of the planes. The airport said flights were being directed to other taxiways, so there was no impact to airport operations. Two patients were treated on the scene by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue for minor injuries and did not require medical transport. UPS confirmed that one of its aircraft was involved in the collision, saying its crew was safe.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Daily Wire both mention the FAA’s statement about the wingtip of the Copa flight striking the nose of the UPS plane, while FOX News and The New York Post describe the collision as the wing clipping the nose. The Guardian and The Daily Wire attribute the collision to the Copa flight taxiing to the gate and the UPS flight taxiing for departure to Bogotá, Colombia. The New York Post and FOX News include a direct quote from the UPS pilot saying, “Yeah, we went too far and he clipped us with his wing,” which is not present in The Guardian or The Daily Wire. The Guardian and The Daily Wire do not include the audio exchange between the pilots and air traffic controllers that FOX News and The New York Post report.

Sources The Guardian · ABC News · Newsweek · FOX News · New York Post · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout

President Trump is traveling to Asia this week to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a high-stakes trilateral summit. The trip to China marks Trump's second visit this year and comes as the president and his party face backlash from voters in recent midterm elections. The meeting is expected to be symbolic rather than substantive, with discussions likely focusing on nuclear weapons and the Iran war. Trump will also attend the ASEAN summit in the Philippines before heading to China. The White House confirmed the meeting, though it does not expect any agreement on denuclearization. The meeting is also seen as a political move for Trump, who has been seeking to reposition himself after the midterm losses.

The trilateral summit is set to take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. The White House and Kremlin have confirmed the gathering, with nuclear weapons and the war involving Iran expected to be among the subjects discussed. The meeting comes less than three weeks after Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections, leaving Trump facing a changed political landscape. The White House has said Trump intends to discuss reducing nuclear arsenals with Xi and Putin, though no agreement is expected. The meeting is also seen as an opportunity for Trump to present himself as a leader capable of bringing together the world's major nuclear powers.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that Trump will meet with Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, with the expectation of low major deals or pronouncements. CBS News states that the meeting is the first trilateral of its kind and that the White House confirmed the meeting on Friday. Newsweek adds that the meeting is historic and brings together the leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers. The Guardian notes that European leaders have expressed reservations about the summit, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warning against major concessions over Ukraine. NPR also mentions the Nvidia scandal and its impact on the meeting, while CBS and Newsweek include details about the controversy surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with Alice Huang.

Sources NPR · CBS News · Newsweek · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

White House lawyer warns Democrats against overreach in oversight investigations

White House Counsel William Scharf sent a letter to California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia on November 9, warning Democrats against running afoul of their constitutional limits on investigations and subpoenas. The letter emphasized the "foundational limits that the Constitution imposes on congressional investigations and subpoenas" and suggested that Democratic actions could cross into criminal misconduct. Garcia responded by stating that Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight under Article I of the Constitution. The letter came a week after Democrats issued statements and social media posts calling for subpoenas and impeachment trials for Trump administration officials following the 2026 midterms.

Scharf told Fox News Sunday that Democrats’ intent to investigate the Trump administration is "out of pettiness," arguing that such efforts must be tied to a "legitimate legislative purpose" rather than self-aggrandizement or threatening behavior. He warned that if Democrats continue with their approach, they would face a "vigorous response" from the White House and the Department of Justice. Legal experts from across the political spectrum suggested that while the administration can challenge individual subpoenas, criminal prosecutions would face a higher legal bar.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that legal experts, including Ilya Shapiro of the Manhattan Institute, suggested that while the White House can challenge subpoenas, criminal prosecutions would face a higher bar. Washington Examiner mentions that Scharf promised a "vigorous response" to Democrats’ oversight threats but does not include the legal expert commentary. The Daily Caller states that Scharf called Garcia’s intent to investigate the administration "out of pettiness" and warned of legal action, but does not mention the legal expert analysis provided by FOX News.

Sources FOX News · Washington Examiner · The Daily Caller

SpaceX launches Starship test flight with partial success

SpaceX conducted its 15th test flight of the Starship rocket on Friday, November 13, 2026, from its Starbase facility in Texas. The mission lasted 22 hours, with the rocket reaching orbit and deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites. The upper stage of the rocket, known as Starship, successfully returned to the launch site and was caught by mechanical arms on the launch gantry, marking a significant milestone. However, the lower stage, or Super Heavy booster, was diverted to a splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico due to a technical issue, where it exploded before impact. SpaceX had previously successfully caught the Super Heavy booster on three earlier test flights, but this was the first time the upper stage was captured after reaching orbit.

The flight was intended to demonstrate full reusability of the Starship system, with both stages returning to the launch site. While the upper stage was successfully retrieved, the lower stage's failure to be caught represents a setback. SpaceX plans to attempt a catch of the upper stage again in the near future, as part of its ongoing efforts to develop a fully reusable rocket system.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News reports that the technical problem preventing the return-to-launch-pad capture of the booster was not immediately known, while BBC and The Guardian attribute the diversion to a guidance, navigation, and control (GNC) system triggering the no-go due to the booster not being in the correct position. The Hill and NPR state that the booster was diverted due to a detected guidance problem, with NPR adding that the engines stopped firing too soon. BBC and The Guardian mention that Elon Musk noted the booster was "slightly low on fuel," a detail not included in CBS News or The Hill. The Daily Wire does not mention the technical problem or the fuel issue, focusing instead on the significance of the attempt.

Sources CBS News · BBC · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · NPR · The Hill

Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment

A federal judge on Saturday issued a temporary restraining order blocking the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course, which is located near the White House. The order, issued by U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, delays any work on the redevelopment project until at least November 28, 2026. The administration had planned to close the site on November 15 to begin renovations. The plaintiffs, including the DC Preservation League and two local golfers, argued that the closure would irreparably harm the public interest and change the character of the accessible golf course. Trump had previously announced the closure date on social media, linking it to the renovation plans.

Reyes noted that Trump's public statements suggested the closure was final and that the National Park Service would close the park to implement the plan, which supported the plaintiffs' request for a stop-work order. The judge ruled that the government must keep the park and golf course open during the hours they were accessible to the public as of November 14, 2026, but did not require active management of the site. The Justice Department stated that the order does not prevent planning for a world-class golf course.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and New York Post both report that the judge issued a temporary restraining order blocking the closure of the park and golf course, while The Hill and Newsweek emphasize the judge's skepticism of the administration's safety arguments. The Hill and Newsweek note that the judge found the government's justifications for closure—such as safety concerns and lack of an operator—were likely pretextual. BBC and The Hill mention that the administration had cut down hundreds of trees without prior notice, which led to an earlier court order halting tree removal. Washington Examiner highlights that the judge grilled the Trump administration's lawyers over the planned closure, expressing skepticism toward the DOJ's rationale.

Sources NPR · Washington Examiner · New York Post · BBC · The Hill · Newsweek

Blumenthal calls for Lutnick’s resignation over Nvidia scandal

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to resign following reports that he shielded Nvidia from federal oversight, which emerged after the tech giant’s CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned. Huang stepped down after allegations surfaced of his infidelity, including an affair with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed employee suspected of being a Chinese spy. The scandal has raised national security concerns about what Trump officials, including Lutnick, knew about the possible espionage. Blumenthal criticized Lutnick in a social media post, accusing him of “malign self-enriching malfeasance” that put “personal profit above public interest.” He argued that allowing China access to Nvidia’s advanced chips endangered both national security and economic competitiveness.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has publicly criticized the Commerce Department for failing to act against Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company linked to the alleged spy. Bessent said multiple agencies, including Treasury, War, and State, had supported placing Megaspeed on an export control list for months, but Commerce did not act. He emphasized that “Commerce has the pen,” and the department must explain its internal processes. Bessent also shifted focus from Huang’s personal conduct to whether Nvidia adequately monitored its customers and prevented technology from reaching unauthorized buyers.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill and Slate both report that Blumenthal called for Lutnick’s resignation, but Slate attributes this to Blumenthal’s social media post and adds that he emphasized the “costs of corruption.” The Hill does not mention Blumenthal’s emphasis on “costs of corruption.” The Free Press and The Daily Wire both mention that Bessent shifted focus from Huang’s personal conduct to whether Nvidia failed to monitor its customers, but The Free Press adds that this is part of a broader theory of “brazen regulatory capture” involving Huang’s access to Trump. The New York Post and The Daily Wire both report that Bessent confronted Lutnick during a White House Situation Room meeting, but The New York Post adds that the Commerce Department denied the confrontation took place, while The Daily Wire notes that the department later stated Lutnick agreed to testify voluntarily.

Sources The Hill · Slate · BBC · The Free Press · New York Post · The Daily Wire

Bomb found near ethanol plant in central Illinois forces evacuations

A bomb was discovered near the BioUrja Renewables ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois, on Friday, prompting a mandatory evacuation of residents within a one-mile radius. Authorities confirmed the device was rendered safe by bomb technicians, though searches for additional threats continued. Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon described the situation as a "credible threat" and emphasized the need for public patience during the investigation. The FBI and other federal agencies were involved in the investigation, with officials stating no arrests had been made and no injuries reported. Evacuation orders were lifted on Saturday afternoon, allowing residents to return to their homes and businesses.

The incident led to the closure of many streets in the area and the establishment of temporary shelters for displaced residents. Local officials, including Peoria Mayor Rita Ali, expressed concern over the presence of highly combustible chemicals at the plant. The evacuation affected both Peoria and the neighboring city of East Peoria, with some events, such as a hockey game and a Comic Con, delayed or canceled due to the situation.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and The Guardian both mention that the evacuation order was lifted on Saturday afternoon, but The Guardian specifies the time as 1.25pm local time, while NPR does not provide a specific time. The Guardian also notes that the evacuation zone extended into East Peoria, which NPR does not mention. The New York Post states the suspicious package was discovered at 1 p.m. on Friday, while ABC News and CBS News report it was found at approximately 2 p.m. on Friday. The Guardian and CBS News both mention that the mayor described the plant as having "ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals," while NPR and the New York Post attribute this statement to the mayor without specifying the outlet. The Washington Examiner reports that the evacuation order was lifted in the afternoon, but does not specify the exact time, while The Guardian and CBS News provide more precise times.

Sources NPR · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · ABC News · CBS News · New York Post

New York Republican says Stephen Miller can leverage MAGA reputation to cut immigration deal

Rep. Nick LaLota (R-NY) this week pushed back against the idea that President Donald Trump’s move to name Stephen Miller his White House chief of staff put a possible immigration deal at risk. Trump first suggested he would be open to crafting legislation with Democrats on an immigration deal after dismal results trickled in for Republicans on election night. However, the president’s appointment of Miller, a known immigration hardliner, as chief of staff triggered concerns that any compromise was unlikely. The Daily Wire reported that Miller’s new memo outlined stricter rules for White House staff engaging with lobbyists, signaling a shift in how the administration would handle external influence.

The Nation highlighted the midterms as a revolt against ICE, noting that voters’ disgust with Trump’s immigration policies was evident. The article emphasized the broader implications of Trump’s policies, including the ICE crackdown in Minneapolis and the administration’s authoritarian tendencies. The Dispatch also mentioned Trump’s move to name Miller as chief of staff, suggesting it may have been an attempt to dangle immigration reform in front of the new Democratic majority.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire both mention Miller’s new memo and its implications for lobbying, but only The Daily Wire attributes the memo to Miller directly. The Nation and The Dispatch focus on the broader political implications of Trump’s appointment, with The Nation emphasizing the ICE crackdown and the midterms as a revolt against it. The Dispatch also notes Trump’s potential motives for the appointment, while The Nation attributes the administration’s authoritarian tendencies to Trump’s policies. The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire do not mention the ICE crackdown or the midterms as a revolt against it.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Nation · The Daily Wire · The Federalist · Mother Jones · The Dispatch

No source labeled center or lean-left covered this story.

U.S. loses measles elimination status

The United States has lost its measles elimination status, according to multiple international health organizations. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) determined that sustained measles transmission has occurred for more than 12 months, marking the first time since 2000 that the U.S. has not met the elimination criteria. The decision follows a surge in measles cases, with over 5,400 confirmed infections reported in 2026, more than double the number from 2025. The majority of cases are in unvaccinated individuals, and public health officials emphasize that vaccination rates must remain above 95% to maintain herd immunity.

The loss of elimination status signifies that measles is now endemic in the U.S., spreading in pockets of unvaccinated communities. Pennsylvania has been the epicenter of the outbreak, with over 1,500 cases and six measles-associated deaths reported. The CDC notes that these numbers are likely undercounts due to limited testing and underreporting of mild cases. The Infectious Diseases Society of America called the loss of status a "tragedy," highlighting the preventable nature of the outbreak and the potential long-term health impacts on infants infected this year.

Where the accounts differ

Axios and CBS News both report that the CDC tallied 5,412 cases in 2026, while The Hill states the number is over 5,400. Axios and CBS News also mention that the CDC has confirmed six deaths, whereas The Hill reports 10 deaths, with the CDC's data being incomplete. NPR and CBS News note that the outbreak in Utah surpassed the one-year mark in June, while Axios and Washington Examiner do not specify the timing of the Utah outbreak. The Hill and NPR attribute the resurgence of measles to the Trump administration's vaccine misinformation and funding cuts, while Axios and CBS News cite declining vaccination rates and public skepticism as key factors. Washington Examiner does not mention specific numbers or attributions beyond the PAHO decision.

Sources Axios · The Hill · CBS News · Washington Examiner · NPR

No source labeled left or right covered this story.

Rubio warns International Criminal Court: 'Stop quoting laws to men with swords' as 2028 speculation grows

Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered a speech at the Federalist Society’s National Lawyers Convention, warning the International Criminal Court (ICC) that its rulings carry no force over Americans. He invoked the Roman general Pompey’s response to those citing their city’s charters against his legions: “Stop quoting laws to men with swords.” The line drew laughter, and Rubio joked that the words were not politically correct. The speech, which followed the GOP’s midterm losses, was seen by some as a potential preview of a 2028 presidential campaign. Rubio accused the ICC and its global-bureaucracy allies of making themselves “judge and jury and executioner of the international order” while answering to no one. He argued that international law is a weapon of a global elite, used against U.S. foreign policy decisions. The speech also touched on America’s founding principles, framing them as rooted in ambition and expansion.

Rubio’s remarks were echoed in other outlets, with The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller reporting on his warning to the ICC and his critique of global institutions. The Hill noted that Rubio’s off-script remarks included a lighter touch on culture issues and a focus on America’s founding ideals. The Washington Examiner highlighted Rubio’s speech as a move to bolster conservative spirits after the midterm losses, while also noting the speculation about a potential 2028 presidential run.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill reports that Rubio’s remarks included a lighter touch on culture issues and a focus on America’s founding ideals, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller emphasize his warning to the ICC and critique of global institutions. The Washington Examiner notes Rubio’s speech as a move to bolster conservative spirits after the midterm losses, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller highlight the ICC warning and global institutions critique. The Hill also mentions Rubio’s off-script remarks and a prepared speech that included a more confrontational tone, which is not detailed in The Daily Wire or The Daily Caller.

Sources The Hill · FOX News · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-left or left covered this story.

Russia is setting traps in Ukraine talks, EU foreign policy chief warns

The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” during peace talks with Ukraine and Russia. She emphasized that Russia is trying to shift focus from its aggression by discussing European security. The talks, held in Abu Dhabi, involved Ukraine, Russia, and the US, with Russia reviving its demand for a total overhaul of European security, a proposal previously rejected in 2021. European leaders have stressed the need for a ceasefire before negotiations and highlighted existing security agreements that Russia has violated.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged European allies to decide who will represent the continent in negotiations, but there is no consensus on a single representative. The EU has proposed a team including EU institutions and E5 countries (Britain, France, Germany, Italy, and Poland). The US, through Jared Kushner, has called for Europe’s inclusion, but Russia has not yet confirmed participation. The Kremlin has stated it will consider European involvement only after understanding their intentions.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, called Russia’s security demands a “trap” to divert attention from its aggression, while Al Jazeera describes the situation as Ukraine being pushed into talks due to dire circumstances and Russia’s confidence in its position. The BBC highlights the Kremlin’s push for a new European security architecture, including the “draft treaties” from 2021, which the Guardian and CBS News also mention. CBS News adds that Jared Kushner is facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Russia, a detail not included in the other accounts.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera · BBC · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

New York City building collapse kills eight, sparks investigation into neighboring construction site

A three-story building collapsed in Brooklyn on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, killing at least eight people and injuring 18 others. The incident occurred on Flatbush Avenue, where emergency responders worked to recover bodies and locate survivors. Video from inside the building captured the moment of the collapse, showing a family's apartment breaking apart. The New York City Mayor, Zohran Mamdani, confirmed the deaths and stated that an investigation is underway. The Department of Buildings is reviewing construction activities at the site and neighboring properties.

The Brooklyn District Attorney’s Office has launched a criminal investigation into the incident, following reports of prior construction violations and a stop-work order issued at the adjacent property. The owner of the neighboring property, Robert Fischman, sent a letter to nearby landlords in June informing them of excavation work. The Department of Buildings cited the contractor, N Tech Design of America, for failing to install safety precautions, including netting and sheds, which were part of the approved plans.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that the adjacent property, 2621 Bedford Ave., had a stop-work order issued in March and that excavation work was ongoing at the time of the collapse. The Guardian notes that officials identified the eight victims and that cracks in the building were reported to the Department of Buildings prior to the collapse. CBS News states that the collapsed building had 98 open violations and that the adjacent contractor, Townhouse Builders, was sued 67 times since 2012. FOX News also mentions that the contractor left the site by late April or early May, months before the collapse, while CBS News attributes the stop-work order violation to Townhouse Builders and notes that the violation was addressed in May.

Sources FOX News · The Guardian · CBS News
